articles.title: Urgent appeal to find woman after suspected human tissue discovered in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Police fear a woman who may have recently given birth needs urgent medical attention after a discovery near Watkins Street and Charter Street, off Kingsway.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS | ONGOING AND DEVELOPING STORY. This report will be updated when further verified information becomes available.

Detectives are trying to find a woman who may need urgent medical attention after suspected human tissue was discovered off Kingsway in Rochdale.

Greater Manchester Police said evidence found near the junction of Watkins Street and Charter Street suggests a woman may have recently given birth. Officers were called shortly before 9am on Thursday 22 October.

Police have been examining the scene and carrying out enquiries. Their priority is to find the woman and make sure she is safe and well.

Detective Inspector Daniel Daly, from GMP's Rochdale CID, said: “She may be in need of urgent medical attention, and she is our absolute priority at the moment - that is why we are asking anyone with information to contact us.”

Anyone with information, or who may have seen a woman in distress, should call 101 and quote incident number 684 of 22/10/2026.

Information can also be reported online or through GMP's LiveChat service at https://www.gmp.police.uk. Alternatively, contact Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.

DI Daly asked the public not to speculate: “We would ask that people don't speculate on the circumstances of this discovery as it hinders our investigation and is upsetting for those involved.”

The information in this report comes from Greater Manchester Police's appeal issued on 22 October 2026. Police have not confirmed further circumstances in that appeal.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Rejects Takeaway Application on Health Grounds
articles.excerpt: Plans for a new takeaway at 159 Yorkshire Street in Rochdale have been rejected by the council due to concerns over public health and the existing number of fast-food outlets in the area.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has refused an application for a new takeaway at 159 Yorkshire Street, citing health concerns related to the high number of existing fast-food establishments in the area. The proposal, submitted by Sheeraz Ahmed, aimed to convert the former Ria Money Transfer shop into a takeaway primarily focused on collection and delivery.

The application detailed plans for a business serving a variety of hot food products, including burgers, fried chicken, pizzas, kebabs, desserts, waffles, and milkshakes. It included internal alterations to create customer serving areas, food preparation spaces, and cooking facilities. The proposed opening hours were set from 11am to 11pm, and the establishment was expected to create four new jobs.

However, the council's planning officer raised concerns regarding the potential impact on local eating habits. The Public Health officer noted that the application would increase the availability of food high in fat, salt, and sugar. Furthermore, it was highlighted that a health impact assessment had not been conducted, leading to the recommendation that the development should not be approved.

This decision reflects ongoing efforts by Rochdale Council to manage the proliferation of fast-food outlets in the town centre, aiming to promote healthier eating habits among residents. The refusal of this application may influence future proposals for similar establishments in the area.

Sheeraz Ahmed applied to Rochdale Council for permission to turn a shop into a fast-food takeaway at 159 Yorkshire Street, Rochdale. The site had most recently been home to Ria Money Transfer. In documents submitted with the application, Building Design Services said: “The proposal seeks to introduce a takeaway business operating primarily as a collection and delivery-based food establishment serving a variety of hot food products, including burgers, fried chicken, pizzas, kebabs, desserts, waffles and milkshakes. “The proposed development would involve internal alterations to facilitate the operation of the takeaway, including the provision of customer serving areas, food preparation spaces, cooking facilities, staff welfare facilities and ancillary storage areas. “The premises would operate as a takeaway only establishment with no internal seating proposed for customers.” The proposed opening hours were from 11am to 11pm and the takeaway would have created four jobs. But the application raised concerns about people’s eating habits and the number of fast-food restaurants and takeaways already in the area. A planning officer’s report referenced the council’s Public Health officer, who noted: “The planning application will increase the availability of food high in fat, salt, and sugar, and a health impact assessment has not been carried out, and as such I request that the development is not approved. READ MORE: Town centre reclaims Britain in Bloom crown “From a Public Health perspective, applications for fast-food outlets should be refused in locations where there is evidence that a concentration of such uses is having an adverse impact on local health, pollution or anti-social-behaviour, or where they are within walking distance of schools and other places where children and young people congregate.” The planning officer added: “Public Health also identifies that obesity levels within both Rochdale and the Central Rochdale Ward exceed national averages and concludes that the proposal would further increase access to unhealthy food choices within an area already experiencing poor health outcomes. “Public Health has further advised that no health impact assessment has been undertaken and that the application has not demonstrated that the proposal would not have an adverse impact on health outcomes.” Refusing the application, the council said: “The proposal would increase the proportion of hot-food takeaway premises within Yorkshire Street Local Centre to approximately 21.7% of commercial ground-floor units, exceeding the 20% threshold set out within the council’s adopted Guidelines and Standards for Hot Food Takeaways SPD. “The Director of Public Health and Communities has identified that there are already 13 hot-food takeaway premises within 400 metres of the application site and 30 such premises within the ward and has provided evidence that obesity levels within both Rochdale and Central Rochdale Ward exceed national averages. “The proposal would further increase the concentration of hot-food takeaway uses within an area where adverse health outcomes have been identified. “Insufficient evidence has been submitted to demonstrate that the proposed development would not contribute to those identified health concerns or to justify a departure from the council’s adopted policy approach.” SUPPORT THE ROCHDALE TIMES: FOLLOW US ON FACEBOOK Got a story? articles.title: Doorman Highlights Normalisation of Racial Abuse After Incident at Ko-Ko Lounge
articles.excerpt: Jawad Ali, a doorman at Ko-Ko Lounge in Rochdale, has raised concerns about the increasing normalisation of racial abuse following a recent incident involving a club-goer.
articles.content_html:
A doorman at Ko-Ko Lounge in Rochdale has raised concerns about the normalisation of racial abuse after witnessing a disturbing incident on Saturday night. Jawad Ali, 20, reported that a woman became aggressive and shouted racial slurs at a black security guard when asked to move away from an exit.

The incident, captured on video and shared widely online, shows the woman making derogatory gestures towards the guard. Ali, who was working for Protective One Security at the time, described the behaviour as "disgusting" and stated that he now expects such incidents during his shifts.

Greater Manchester Police confirmed they have received a report regarding the incident and are currently conducting inquiries. Ali alleged that the woman also directed racial abuse towards him before the video was recorded.

This incident raises significant concerns about the treatment of security staff and the prevalence of racial abuse in nightlife settings. As investigations continue, it highlights the need for greater awareness and action against such behaviour.

articles.excerpt: Martlet Kitchen, located in Rochdale, has been ranked among the top-rated restaurants globally, celebrating its second anniversary with an international award.

Martlet Kitchen, a restaurant in Rochdale, has recently achieved international recognition by being ranked among the top-rated restaurants globally. This accolade comes as the establishment celebrates its second birthday, marking a significant milestone in its journey since opening.

The restaurant has been rated in the top 10 percent of all establishments on TripAdvisor, highlighting its commitment to quality and customer satisfaction. Martlet Kitchen is known for its focus on using top-quality local ingredients, which has contributed to its growing reputation in the culinary scene.

Local supplier Grandpa Greene’s plays a vital role in providing ingredients for Martlet Kitchen, further emphasising the restaurant's dedication to supporting local businesses. The restaurant aims to continue its success and is looking forward to achieving more accolades in the future.

In addition to Martlet Kitchen, other local establishments such as Shibden Mill Inn and The Fleece Inn have also been recognised with 2 AA rosettes, showcasing the high standard of dining available in the area. Martlet Kitchen prides itself on delivering excellent service, which has undoubtedly played a part in its recent achievements.

articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council Invites Feedback on Proposed Customer Access Strategy
articles.excerpt: Residents are encouraged to share their views on the proposed Customer Access & Experience Strategy, which aims to enhance how the public interacts with the Council over the next five years.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has launched a consultation inviting residents to provide feedback on its proposed Customer Access & Experience Strategy for the next five years. The strategy aims to simplify how residents contact the Council and ensure they receive consistent support, whether online, by phone, or in person.

The Council has identified six priorities for enhancing customer access and nine pledges detailing what residents can expect from the service. The aim is to create a seamless experience for users, allowing them to receive assistance without needing to navigate the Council's organisational structure. The Council emphasises the importance of making it easy for individuals to access the right help, especially during challenging times.

Residents can review the draft strategy and related documents, including the Equality Impact Assessment and Sustainability Impact Assessment, on the Council's consultation hub. The Council is keen to know if the proposed priorities resonate with the community and whether any aspects have been overlooked. The consultation documents are available for review and can be accessed through the Council's website.

The consultation is open now, and residents are encouraged to participate to help shape the final version of the strategy. Feedback can be submitted through the Council's website until the consultation period closes. This initiative represents an opportunity for the community to influence how the Council interacts with its residents over the coming years.

articles.title: Chris Cheap Appointed Managing Director of Atom Valley’s Northern Gateway Regeneration
articles.excerpt: Chris Cheap has been appointed as the new managing director of the Atom Valley Northern Gateway Mayoral Development Corporation, overseeing significant regeneration projects in Rochdale and surrounding areas.
articles.content_html:
The Atom Valley Northern Gateway Mayoral Development Corporation (MDC) has appointed Chris Cheap as its new managing director. This appointment is part of a broader initiative aimed at revitalising the Atom Valley area, which spans across Bury, Oldham, and Rochdale, focusing on advanced manufacturing, innovation, housing, and infrastructure.

The Northern Gateway is a pivotal component of the Atom Valley Mayoral Development Zone, which aims to drive economic growth and reindustrialisation in the region. Recently, the Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre (SMMC), a 30,000 sq ft facility located within the 25-acre Atom Valley Innovation District at Kingsway Park in Rochdale, was completed, marking an important step in the development.

One of the key projects under the Northern Gateway will enhance highway connections between the site and the M66 and M60 motorways. This improvement is essential for unlocking further phases of development and complements ongoing works to increase capacity at the nearby Simister Island.

Chris Cheap brings nearly 23 years of experience from Avison Young, where he held various leadership roles. His expertise will be crucial as the MDC seeks to implement its ambitious plans for the Northern Gateway, which is expected to play a significant role in the UK government's Northern Growth Strategy.

Our Mayoral Development Corporations are turning ambition into action. “They get development moving much faster – by aligning land, infrastructure, investment and decision-making so complex projects can be delivered at pace and at scale. “Northern Gateway is no different. Alongside housing and infrastructure, its focus on advanced manufacturing and innovation means it’s set to be significant not just for Greater Manchester, but for the country too.” Northern Gateway has seen more than £100 million of public funding spent and committed to date, including more than £50 million of GM Good Growth Fund support allocated in March, 2026, by Greater Manchester Combined Authority to support transport improvements. articles.title: Rochdale and Grimsby Town Share Points in 2-2 Draw at Crown Oil Arena
articles.excerpt: A late equaliser from Ian Henderson secured a point for Rochdale in a thrilling 2-2 draw against Grimsby Town in League Two on October 20, 2026.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale AFC salvaged a point in a dramatic 2-2 draw against Grimsby Town at the Crown Oil Arena on Tuesday, October 20, 2026. The match saw veteran striker Ian Henderson come off the bench to score an equaliser in the 88th minute, preventing Grimsby from claiming all three points after they had taken the lead in the second half.

The game began with both teams eager to break their recent poor form. Rochdale took the lead in the 38th minute when Dajaune Brown scored following a well-placed cross from Glenn Middleton. However, Grimsby responded strongly after the break, with Kieran Green equalising in the 57th minute after a saved header from Andy Cook. The visitors then took the lead in the 72nd minute through Jamie Walker, who capitalised on a partially cleared corner.

Despite trailing, Rochdale continued to press for a goal. Their persistence paid off when Henderson, who had been introduced as a substitute, headed in a cross from Charlie Tasker to level the score just before full-time. This late goal marked a significant moment for Rochdale, who had recently suffered a defeat against Crewe Alexandra, ending a five-match unbeaten run.

The draw leaves Rochdale in 13th place in League Two with 15 points, while Grimsby Town, who ended a four-match losing streak, sit just behind in 15th with 14 points. Both teams will look to build on this result in their upcoming fixtures as they aim to improve their standings in the league.

articles.title: Rochdale House Prices Rise to £211,000 in August 2026
articles.excerpt: The average house price in Rochdale increased by 3.3% over the past year, while private rents saw a significant rise of 8.8%, according to the latest figures from the Office for National Statistics.
articles.content_html:
The average house price in Rochdale reached £211,000 in August 2026, reflecting a 3.3% increase from the previous year, according to data released by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). This rise is notably higher than the average increase of 2.2% observed across the North West during the same period.

In addition to house prices, private rents in Rochdale also saw a substantial increase, with the average rent climbing to £859 in September 2026. This marks an annual rise of 8.8%, compared to £790 in September 2025, again outpacing the North West's average increase of 5.7%.

For first-time buyers, the average price paid for a home was £191,000 in August 2026, which is a 3.4% increase from the previous year's average of £184,000. Homes purchased with a mortgage had an average price of £215,000, also reflecting a 3.3% rise from £208,000 in August 2025.

These figures indicate a continuing trend of rising housing costs in Rochdale, which may impact affordability for local residents. The ONS advises that local housing data can be more variable due to the smaller number of properties involved, and they recommend looking at trends over a longer period for a clearer picture.

articles.title: Plans to Develop Wasteland Around Rochdale Train Station Confirmed
articles.excerpt: Plans to transform the wasteland surrounding Rochdale train station into a usable space have been confirmed, marking a significant step towards improving the area.
articles.content_html:
Plans to develop the wasteland around Rochdale train station have been confirmed. Local authorities aim to enhance the environment and accessibility for commuters and residents.

This initiative is part of ongoing efforts to revitalise the area, which has been largely neglected in recent years. The local council stated that the project will improve aesthetic appeal and provide additional facilities for the community.

Specific details regarding the timeline and nature of the developments are yet to be announced. Stakeholders are optimistic that this project will lead to increased foot traffic and economic activity in the vicinity of the station.

Residents and commuters are encouraged to monitor the progress of this project, as it is expected to positively impact local transport and community engagement.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The wasteland around Rochdale train station is finally being put to use - Manchester Evening News ‌ ‌ Skip to main content Manchester Evening News: Number one for news, opinion, sport & celebrity news The wasteland around Rochdale train station is finally being put to use The regeneration around the railway station is part of a wider vision to improve the flow of the down and drive investment Add to preferred sources Comments News George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter 06:13, 21 Oct 2026 View 4 Images Land surrounding Rochdale train station (Image: LDRS) A scheme which would transform the gateway into Rochdale is making significant progress, town hall bosses say. ‌ ‌ Some 81 two, three-and four-bedroom homes are currently under construction on vacant land next to Rochdale ’s Central Retail Park. This forms part of a wider scheme to create a connection between the train station and the town centre. ‌ The wider regeneration of the area around Rochdale railway station also involves the creation of a new public square in front of the station and 33 new apartments on a brownfield site on the corner of Maclure Road and Station Road. ‌ Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter The train station in Rochdale was once a hub for industrial business generations ago, so the distance between the station and the town centre was purposeful separation. But as times changed, society changed and the station suddenly started transporting people, not goods. This is why there is an idea to improve access and avenues from the station and the main hub of the town. This 81-home development, known as John Rennie Place, in honour of the late Scottish Civil engineer who masterminded the Rochdale Canal, got under way in November last year, and is due for completion in December 2027. ‌ View 4 Images The former Central Retail Park site development under construction (Image: Rochdale council) The project, approved years ago, was unlocked following a successful bid for £15m from the government’s Community Regeneration Partnerships Fund. The transformation has been on the cards for a long time, but the local authority struggled to get the investment until last year. ‌ The properties will be the first affordable net zero homes delivered as part of a housing scheme supported by the council. The local authority says the development is already delivering benefits to the local economy and community. Contractor Willmott Dixon, working on behalf of the council, has already spent £3.3m with local civil engineering firm, Hovington Ltd, and supported a total of 95 weeks of apprenticeship and T-Level training, including three T-Level placements from Hopwood Hall College. ‌ Don't let an algorithm decide what Manchester news you see - click here to add the MEN as your preferred Google source Seven local people are also employed on the project, including two people who were previously unemployed, with the council’s work and skills team supporting the recruitment. ‌ Tommy Patterson, 22, from Middleton , is one of the local people working on the new homes. He said: “I had been out of work for six months when the job centre arranged for me to get my CSCS card and that led to me securing a scaffolding apprenticeship here on site. Councillor Danny Meredith, cabinet member for housing and regeneration at Rochdale Borough Council, said: ”We want local people and businesses to feel the benefit of local projects and it’s great to see that these benefits are already being felt on this development before a single house has even been completed. ‌ View 4 Images Councillor Danny Meredith looking across the former Rochdale Central Retail Park site (Image: Rochdale council) “By ensuring that social value is embedded in our procurement system, we’re making sure that local people are invested in the extensive regeneration which is taking place on their doorstep and are benefitting from the economic transformation we’re spearheading across the borough. That’s how it should be and how it will continue to be.” Article continues below Work to create 142 apartments next to the new homes is ongoing, with the procurement of a delivery partner expected to get underway soon. articles.title: Rochdale Schools Benefit from Tesco's Free Fruit and Veg Programme
articles.excerpt: Schools across Greater Manchester, including those in Rochdale, received over 750,000 portions of fruit and vegetables through Tesco's initiative, promoting healthier eating among pupils.
articles.content_html:
Schools across Greater Manchester, including those in Rochdale, have received a total of 750,600 portions of fruit and vegetables as part of Tesco's Free Fruit & Veg for Schools programme. This initiative, now in its third year, aims to encourage healthier eating habits among children.

The produce, which weighed more than 60,000 kilograms, was distributed to schools throughout the region. Apples were the most popular choice, with approximately 221,000 portions consumed, followed by bananas at around 103,000 portions. Satsumas and clementines also featured prominently, with about 88,000 portions provided.

Since its launch, the programme has supplied nearly 20 million portions of fruit and vegetables across the UK, benefiting up to 186,000 pupils. According to a recent impact report, 98% of teachers reported that the initiative encouraged students to try a wider variety of fruits, while 94% noted improvements in student behaviour.

While specific figures for Rochdale schools were not disclosed, the overall success of the programme highlights its positive impact on children's nutrition and well-being. As the scheme continues, it is expected to reach even more schools and students in the coming year.

articles.title: Office of Rail and Road Rejects Proposal for Extra Rochdale to London Train Services
articles.excerpt: The Office of Rail and Road has turned down a proposal for additional train services from Rochdale to London, citing concerns over delays and capacity on the West Coast Main Line.
articles.content_html:
Plans to enhance the rail link between Rochdale and London have been rejected once again. The Office of Rail and Road (ORR) announced that it had turned down proposals from Lumo to operate up to four additional return services from Rochdale to Euston on weekdays and Saturdays, and three services on Sundays.

Rochdale MP Paul Waugh had supported the bid, describing it as a "game-changing opportunity" for the borough and the wider North West. However, the ORR's assessment concluded that adding more trains to the already congested West Coast Main Line would likely lead to increased delays and cancellations for passengers. This decision follows a similar rejection of Lumo's application last year, with the ORR stating that the capacity and performance of the southern section of the line had not materially changed since then.

An external review commissioned by the ORR corroborated these findings, indicating that the current timetable must allow for recovery time during disruptions to minimise delays. The ORR emphasised the importance of maintaining service reliability for existing passengers.

The rejection of this proposal means that residents of Rochdale will not see an increase in direct train services to London in the near future, which could impact travel options for commuters and those wishing to visit the capital.

Today, the Office of Rail and Road announced it had rejected proposals for new train services which would have seen Lumo operate up to four additional return Rochdale-to-Euston services on weekdays and Saturdays and three services on Sundays . Among those backing calls for the extra services was Rochdale MP Paul Waugh, who called Lumo’s bid to restore six daily direct services between Rochdale and the capital a “game-changing opportunity” for the borough and the wider North West. But the ORR rejected the plans after its assessment found adding more trains to the West Coast Main Line — which also included services to Blackpool and Wrexham — would likely increase delays and cancelled trains for passengers. It said its assessment following detailed and extensive analysis is that the capacity and performance of the southern section of the West Coast Main Line has not materially changed since it rejected a similar application by Lumo last year. An external review commissioned by ORR also supported this conclusion. READ MORE: Police target crime gang’s ‘spider web of criminality’ The ORR said gaps in the current timetable need to provide important space for trains to recover when disruption occurs, minimising delays to passengers. It concluded that adding more services into these windows in the timetable for recovery would reduce that resilience, increasing the risk of disruption spreading to other services and affecting more passengers. Stephanie Tobyn, ORR’s director of strategy, policy and reform, said: “New services, destinations and greater choice can bring real benefits for passengers and communities. “But the West Coast Main Line is already under significant pressure, with performance reflecting limited resilience on a heavily used part of the rail network. “Our detailed analysis has shown that adding more trains to the current timetable would reduce the ability to recover when disruption occurs, increasing the risk of delays spreading and making reliability of the network worse for all passengers.” SUPPORT THE ROCHDALE TIMES: FOLLOW US ON FACEBOOK Got a story? articles.title: Three Rochdale Artists Awarded Free Studio Space to Develop New Work
articles.excerpt: Three emerging artists from Rochdale have been awarded free studio space, along with funding and support, to help establish their creative practices in the area.
articles.content_html:
Three emerging artists from Rochdale have been awarded free studio space as part of an initiative aimed at supporting local talent. The selected artists will also receive materials funding and additional support to develop their work, which is valued at approximately £1,200 per artist.

The initiative is designed to address the lack of financial support for emerging artists and aims to enhance their professional development. Each artist will benefit from a package that includes technical assistance and marketing support, allowing them to establish their creative practices more effectively.

Among the recipients is Madison Marcantonatos, a multidisciplinary artist whose work is expected to reflect her personal experiences and creativity. This support is part of a broader effort to foster creative talent within Rochdale and provide emerging artists with the resources they need to succeed.

The initiative not only aims to support individual artists but also seeks to enrich the local arts scene, encouraging a vibrant community of creativity in Rochdale. The artists will begin their studio time shortly, marking an important step in their artistic journeys.

Image credit: Ella Marshall Three emerging Rochdale artists will receive free studio space, materials funding and support to develop work for a joint exhibition. Richard Street Studios and Breaking Barriers have named Alisha K., Madison Marcantonatos and Georgia Scholes as recipients of support funded by The Haworth Trust. Each artist will receive ten free days at Richard Street Studios, with the studio time valued at an estimated £1,200 per artist. The package also includes a materials budget and technical and marketing support. The scheme aims to help artists establish their practice in Rochdale. Parvez Qadir, artistic director at Breaking Barriers, said, “Rochdale has no shortage of creative talent. What it has lacked is the financial support for artists to take that talent seriously at the start of their careers.” Alisha K., who works with oil paint and pastel, said this would be her first opportunity to work in a professional studio alongside other artists. She said, “By the end, I hope to have pushed my practice further and created a body of work that reflects what I can do.” Multidisciplinary artist Madison Marcantonatos plans to explore nostalgia and her own experiences. She said, “Like many creatives, I’ve been caught up in commercial work, which has left little room for my own practice.” Collage and textile artist Georgia Scholes plans to make a large-scale textile banner celebrating Rochdale’s radical history. She said, “This funding gives me the time to develop my practice and build connections in a creative environment.” The artists’ work will be shown in a joint exhibition at Richard Street Studios in March 2027. articles.title: Secondary school applications close on 31 October: what Rochdale parents need to know
articles.excerpt: The council advises families to list five preferences and apply by Saturday 31 October. Late applications are considered after National Offer Day on 1 March 2027.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale families have until Saturday 31 October 2026 to apply for a secondary school place through the council's online parent portal.

With the deadline approaching, the council advises parents to name five school preferences. Repeating a school, or listing just one, does not improve the chance of securing it.

Applying on time matters. The council says 331 families applied late last year: 51% received their first preference, compared with 87% of applicants who met the deadline. Those figures describe last year's admissions, not a guarantee for this round.

Late applications are considered after National Offer Day, 1 March 2027. Schools do not hold places back for late applicants, so a preferred school may already be full.

Before submitting, read each school's admissions criteria, prospectus and Ofsted report. An on-time application still does not guarantee a preferred place.

Official deadline, guidance and admissions link: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/news/article/675/council-urges-families-to-apply-on-time-for-secondary-school-places

articles.title: Rochdale’s £5m crisis support fund: what help is available this winter and how to ask
articles.excerpt: The council lists help with sudden financial emergencies, housing costs and essential goods. Different schemes have different rules; an award is not automatic.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale residents struggling to afford essentials can ask about support through the council's Crisis and Resilience Fund as winter approaches.

The £5 million programme runs from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027, using Department for Work and Pensions funding. It replaced the Household Support Fund in April. The £5 million is the borough-wide programme budget, not an amount available to each household.

The council lists several routes: Crisis Payments for sudden financial difficulty; Housing Payments for emergency rent or housing costs; the Discretionary Crisis Fund for goods; and Healthy Homes grants for eligible vulnerable residents needing help such as boiler repairs or essential appliances. Each route needs its own eligibility check.

For Crisis Payments, eligible residents can receive a voucher worth up to £75 towards food and energy. Applicants must live in Rochdale borough, be at least 16 and have nobody receiving Child Benefit for them. Applications are allowed once every six months. Apply by calling 01706 923685; the published hours are Monday to Friday, 9am–5pm. Examples of a crisis include fire, flooding, a health emergency or losing employment.

The separate Discretionary Crisis Fund is described as last-resort support. It provides goods rather than cash. Its contact number is 01706 532222 and its email is StrategicHousing@rochdale.gov.uk.

Check the route that matches your circumstances before applying. The main fund page also mentions food vouchers only through the end of the 2026 summer holidays; that wording does not establish a winter voucher entitlement.

Official programme and scheme guidance: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/cost-living/crisis-resilience-fund

articles.title: Rochdale Sleep Out Raises Funds for Homeless Support
articles.excerpt: Fundraisers gathered at Crown Oil Arena for the annual Sleep Out, raising awareness and funds for homelessness initiatives in the community.
articles.content_html:
Fundraisers spent a night outdoors at Rochdale's Crown Oil Arena to raise awareness and vital funds for people experiencing homelessness. This event, the second annual Sleep Out organised by Petrus Communities and RAFC Community Trust, saw supporters from across the borough come together for a common cause.

The money raised will support the Changing Lives initiative, a football programme designed to assist individuals facing homelessness or living in supported accommodation. The initiative aims to enhance participants' mental health, physical well-being, and social inclusion through free football sessions, while also providing personal development opportunities, including pathways into volunteering, education, and employment.

Louise Scriven, Fundraising and Partnerships Coordinator at Petrus, emphasised that the Sleep Out is not about pretending to experience homelessness, but about standing in solidarity with those facing housing insecurities. She noted that last year's event significantly impacted participants, helping them rebuild confidence, forge new friendships, and develop skills to become active community members.

The funds raised from this year's Sleep Out will continue to provide essential accommodation, support, advice, and opportunities for those experiencing homelessness and disadvantage in Rochdale, Oldham, and Burnley. Donations are crucial for sustaining these services and making a difference in the lives of vulnerable individuals in the community.

articles.title: Rochdale Unemployment Claimants Increase to 8,775 in September 2026
articles.excerpt: The number of people claiming unemployment-related benefits in Rochdale rose by 270 in September 2026, marking an increase from the previous month and year.
articles.content_html:
The number of people claiming unemployment-related benefits in Rochdale rose by 270 in September 2026, bringing the total to 8,775. This figure represents 6.0% of residents aged 16 to 64, an increase from 5.8% in August 2026.

In September 2025, the claimant count was slightly lower at 8,625, indicating a year-on-year increase in unemployment claims. The latest figures were published by the Office for National Statistics through Nomis, and the September data is provisional and subject to revision.

The rise in claimants may reflect broader economic challenges affecting the local job market, although specific reasons for the increase have not been detailed in the report. The data is crucial for understanding employment trends in the area and may influence local policy decisions.

Residents and local businesses may feel the impact of this increase, as higher unemployment can affect consumer spending and overall economic activity in Rochdale.

articles.title: Inspector Rules Against Garden Fence Appeal in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: A planning inspector has upheld Rochdale Council's decision to refuse retrospective planning permission for a garden fence at 19 Town House Road, Littleborough, citing its negative impact on the area's character.
articles.content_html:
A planning inspector has ruled against a homeowner's appeal regarding a garden fence at 19 Town House Road, Littleborough. Caterina Buonocore had sought retrospective planning permission for a 1.55-metre high boundary fence, which is approximately twice the height of the original fence. The council had previously rejected her application, leading to the appeal.

In the inspector's decision, it was stated that the main concern was the fence's effect on the character and appearance of the area. The inspector noted that boundary treatments in the locality are typically low-level and visually permeable, contributing to a sense of openness and allowing the greenery in front gardens to be appreciated. The inspector remarked that the existing vegetation helps to soften the street scene, enhancing the area's character.

The inspector further explained that the close-boarded timber fence introduced by the appeal contrasts sharply with the more traditional forms of boundary treatment found in the neighbourhood. Observations made on-site indicated that, due to the prominent corner location, the fence appeared particularly stark and incongruous against the backdrop of traditional stone terraces with lower boundary treatments.

As a result of this ruling, Buonocore may now be required to remove the fence, which could have implications for her property and the surrounding area. The decision underscores the importance of maintaining the character of local neighbourhoods and adhering to planning regulations.

Rochdale Council refused Caterina Buonocore’s application for retrospective planning permission for the 1.55m high boundary fence — about twice the height of the original — around 19 Town House Road, Littleborough. She appealed that decision. But yesterday, a Planning Inspector rejected the appeal, stating: “The main issue is the effect of the appeal development on the character and appearance of the area. “Boundary treatments in the area are typically low-level and visually permeable, contributing to a sense of openness and allowing the soft landscaping within front gardens to remain appreciable. The existing greenery helps to soften the street scene and makes a positive contribution to the character and appearance of the area. “The appeal development introduces a close-boarded timber fence. The height, materials and extensive continuous form of enclosure contrasts with the more open and traditional forms of boundary treatment typically found in the locality. “On site, I observed that due to the prominent corner location, when seen from Park View against the back drop of traditional stone terraces with low-key forms of boundary treatment, the appeal development appears particularly stark and incongruous within the street scene. READ MORE: The fence liked by neighbours — but not planners 19 Town House Road in Littleborough with the previous boundary. Image: Google “It is acknowledged that there is support from neighbours. One neighbour prefers fencing to hedging as they consider it ensures the pavement remains unobstructed. However, this does not justify the identified harm caused by the appeal development. “The appeal development provides additional privacy and security to the occupiers. However, any such benefit does not outweigh the identified harm to the character of the area. “Overall, I find that the appeal development causes harm to the character and appearance of the area and the street scene.” In refusing the original planning application, the council said: “The installed boundary fence constitutes an unsympathetic and visually prominent form of development which inflicts undue harm on the character and appearance of the application property and the immediate street scene. “The development fails to respond positively to its context, does not make a positive contribution to local character and would not be well-designed. articles.title: Ian Henderson's Late Equaliser Secures Draw for Rochdale Against Grimsby
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's Ian Henderson salvaged a point for his team with a late goal in a 2-2 draw against Grimsby Town at the Crown Oil Arena, as manager Ian Watson praised his performance.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale AFC secured a dramatic late equaliser against Grimsby Town in a 2-2 draw at the Crown Oil Arena on Tuesday evening, thanks to a goal from veteran striker Ian Henderson. The 41-year-old came off the bench in the 81st minute, trailing 2-1, and found the net just seven minutes later, turning in a delivery from Charlie Tasker to level the score.

Manager Ian Watson praised Henderson's impact, calling him 'an amazing guy and an amazing footballer'. Watson noted the challenge posed by Grimsby, who had been on a four-game losing streak prior to this match. He remarked on the aggressive style of play from the opposition, which made it difficult for his team to maintain momentum throughout the game.

Rochdale initially took the lead in the first half when Dajaune Brown scored in the 38th minute, following a cross from Glenn Middleton. However, Grimsby responded strongly, with Kieran Green equalising in the 57th minute and Jamie Walker putting them ahead in the 72nd minute. Despite the setback, Henderson's late goal ensured that Rochdale walked away with a point.

The draw leaves both teams reflecting on missed opportunities, with Grimsby manager David Artell expressing disappointment that his side did not secure all three points, despite their strong performance. The match showcased the resilience of Rochdale, particularly in the face of adversity, and highlighted Henderson's continued importance to the team as they look to build on this result in their upcoming fixtures.

articles.title: Lifts at Freehold Tram Stop Out of Service Until Further Notice
articles.excerpt: The lifts at Freehold Tram Stop are currently out of service due to replacement works, affecting journeys towards Manchester and Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
The lifts at Freehold Tram Stop are out of service as of 6:59pm on Sunday, 18 October 2026, due to ongoing lift replacement works. This affects both platforms, with the lift towards Manchester and the lift towards Rochdale currently unavailable.

Passengers are advised to alight at either South Chadderton or Westwood tram stops and use the orange call point located at all stops to request assistance for completing their journeys. For further assistance, customers can contact the helpline at 0161 244 1000, which operates from 7am to 8pm on weekdays and 8am to 8pm on weekends and bank holidays.

The duration of the lift outage is currently unspecified, and no further updates have been provided regarding when the service will resume. Passengers are encouraged to plan their journeys accordingly and allow extra time for travel.

Transport for Greater Manchester apologises for any inconvenience caused by this disruption and is working to resolve the issue as quickly as possible.

articles.title: Rochdale Falls to Crewe in 3-2 Defeat in League Two
articles.excerpt: Crewe Alexandra secured a 3-2 victory over Rochdale, marking a record-breaking start to their league campaign. Manager Lee Bell praised his team's performance and resilience against a strong Rochdale side.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale AFC faced a disappointing defeat against Crewe Alexandra, losing 3-2 in a League Two match on Saturday, October 17. This defeat marked Rochdale's first loss in six league games, despite a spirited effort in the second half.

Crewe took the lead in the 39th minute when Matus Holicek scored with a powerful strike from outside the box, which goalkeeper Sam Waller managed to get a hand to but could not prevent from going in. Jordan Gibson then added to the scoreline with two goals, one just before half-time and another ten minutes into the second half, putting Crewe ahead 3-0.

Rochdale managed to respond with a goal from Joel Tabiner, who inadvertently diverted a cross from Glenn Middleton into his own net in the 65th minute. Aden Flint then scored a header from a cross by substitute Ed Francis in the closing stages, but it was not enough to secure a comeback for the visitors.

The result leaves Rochdale looking to regroup as they prepare for their next fixture, while Crewe continues their unbeaten run, now boasting three consecutive victories. The match was held at Gresty Road, Crewe, and the defeat will be a point of reflection for Rochdale as they aim to improve in their upcoming matches.

articles.title: Harvest Thanksgiving Service to be Held in Rochdale on October 17

Led by Rev’d Ben Somervell, the service will include a sermon based on Psalm 126. Attendees are encouraged to bring donations of tinned and dry packaged foods for the local foodbank, highlighting the importance of community support during challenging times.

articles.title: Broadfield Park Slopes Renovation Celebrated at Rochdale Town Hall
articles.excerpt: A special event at Rochdale Town Hall recognised the contributions of volunteers and partners involved in the restoration of Broadfield Park Slopes, highlighting the project's community impact and heritage significance.
articles.content_html:
A celebration was held at Rochdale Town Hall to honour the individuals and groups who contributed to the renovation of Broadfield Park Slopes. This historic site, located between Rochdale Town Hall and St Chad’s Church, has undergone significant restoration, thanks to the efforts of local volunteers and funding from The National Lottery Heritage Fund.

The event, organised by Polly Brant, Cultural Engagement Officer for Rochdale Council, brought together volunteers, partners, and community members to acknowledge their roles in the project. Guests were treated to a series of films by local filmmaker Jack Grindrod, showcasing the stories and heritage associated with the park's transformation. The films captured the community involvement that played a crucial role in the renovation process.

The evening featured poetry readings by Alende Amisi, a local poet and former young poet in residence, who shared his personal reflections on Rochdale's heritage. His contributions added a personal touch to the event, which celebrated not only the park's restoration but also the community spirit that drove the project forward.

The renovation has restored the historic Packer Spout Fountain, created a new accessible pathway, improved landscaping, and introduced new heritage interpretation. The lower lawn has been terraced to create a natural amphitheatre, providing a new space for activities and events, enhancing the park's role as a community hub.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Town celebrates the people and stories behind Broadfield Park Slopes renovation - Rochdale Times Skip to content LATEST NEWS Town celebrates the people and stories behind Broadfield Park Slopes renovation The people who helped bring Rochdale’s historic Broadfield Park Slopes back to life were celebrated at a special event at Rochdale Town Hall. The celebration, arranged by Polly Brant, Rochdale Council Cultural Engagement officer, brought together volunteers, partners and people who have been involved in the project to recognise what has been achieved and, importantly, the contribution local people have made along the way. Guests watched a series of films created by Rochdale filmmaker Jack Grindrod and Breaking Barriers, capturing the people, stories, heritage and community involvement behind the transformation. The evening also featured poetry readings from Alende Amisi, a poet who grew up in Rochdale and was a young poet in residence during Rochdale’s Town of Culture. Passionate about the town and its heritage, Alende brought a personal perspective to an evening which was as much about Rochdale’s people as its history. A special thank you was also given to the many volunteers who have supported the project, giving their time to archaeological digs, activities and events and helping uncover and share the history of this important part of the town. The Grade II listed Broadfield Park Slopes sit between Rochdale Town Hall and St Chad’s Church and have been restored through a project delivered by Rochdale Development Agency working with Rochdale Borough Council, with funding from The National Lottery Heritage Fund. The work has restored the historic Packer Spout Fountain, created a new accessible pathway, improved landscaping, lighting and CCTV, and introduced new heritage interpretation. The lower lawn has also been terraced, creating a natural amphitheatre and new space for activities and events. READ MORE: Customers flock to opening of new Peacocks store Archaeology and community participation have been a major part of the project. Excavations have uncovered the footings of Charles Kershaw’s 19th century Central Corn Mill, cobbled trackways and the former public weigh station, alongside finds including ceramics, clay smoking pipes, animal bones and glass bottles. Four archaeological digs have taken place, with the wider programme involving schoolchildren, students, volunteers and members of the public. It has included 28 work placement students, 12 archaeological volunteers and a two year schools programme involving 715 pupils. Cllr Sue Smith, portfolio holder for Communities and Co-operation at Rochdale Council, said: “This was a wonderful opportunity to celebrate not just the transformation of the Broadfield Park Slopes, but the people who have made this project so special. “Our volunteers deserve a huge thank you. They have given their time, enthusiasm and energy to this project and have helped us uncover and share more of Rochdale’s history. “It was fantastic to see those stories captured in the films created by Jack Grindrod and Breaking Barriers, and to hear from Alende Amisi, whose passion for Rochdale and its heritage really reflects what this project is about. “The Slopes have been part of Rochdale for generations. We have protected an important part of our heritage, opened it back up for people to enjoy and, crucially, involved our communities in doing it.” The Broadfield Park Slopes are now open to the public, creating a restored green space at the heart of Rochdale’s historic town centre. articles.title: Rochdale man refused permission to appeal Manchester Airport assault sentence
articles.excerpt: Mohammed Fahir Amaaz, from Rochdale, has been refused permission to appeal against his 42-month sentence following assaults at Manchester Airport, according to sources.
articles.content_html:
A Rochdale man jailed after assaulting two police officers and a member of the public at Manchester Airport has been refused permission to appeal against his sentence, according to sources.

Mohammed Fahir Amaaz, 21, was sentenced at Liverpool Crown Court on 26 June 2026 to 42 months in prison. The Crown Prosecution Service confirmed his convictions were for assault occasioning actual bodily harm, assault by beating and assault on an emergency worker.

His renewed application for permission to appeal against sentence was scheduled before the Court of Appeal in London on Friday 16 October. The published court listing placed the case in Court 6 at 10am, under reference 202602577.

Before the hearing, his solicitors, Imran Khan and Partners, said a single judge had refused his initial application on 14 August. His legal team then renewed the application to the full court. Friday’s proceedings concerned permission to challenge his sentence.

The convictions arose from events at Manchester Airport on 23 July 2024. According to the CPS, the incident began when Amaaz assaulted a passenger inside the Terminal 2 Starbucks and continued in another part of the airport when police arrived to arrest him. One officer suffered a broken nose.

The offences for which he was sentenced involved member of the public Abdulkareem Hamzah Abbas Ismaeil, PC Lydia Ward and PC Ellie Cook.

A separate allegation involving PC Zachary Marsden must be distinguished from those convictions. Amaaz and his brother, Muhammad Amaad, also from Rochdale, faced that allegation, but two juries were unable to reach verdicts. In May 2026, the prosecution offered no further evidence and not guilty verdicts were recorded.

The sentence application listed on Friday was in Mohammed Fahir Amaaz’s name. Rochdale Daily will update this report if the court’s detailed reasons or a further statement from his legal representatives become available.

Each business's current rating is on the Food Standards Agency website.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Download ratings data | title Skip to main content Food Standards Agency - Frontpage Navigation Menu UK food hygiene rating data API The food hygiene rating data published at https://ratings.food.gov.uk are available via an application programming interface (API) in XML and JSON formats. This is a free service and there is no need to register to use it. Terms and conditions apply (see link below), and guidance for developers is available. Terms and conditions Read the terms and conditions of using the data and images. About the data The data provides the food hygiene rating or inspection result given to a business and reflect the standards of food hygiene found on the date of inspection or visit by the local authority. Businesses include restaurants, pubs, cafés, takeaways, hotels and other places consumers eat, as well as supermarkets and other food shops. The data are held on behalf of local authorities participating in either the: national Food Hygiene Rating Scheme (FHRS) in England, Northern Ireland and Wales, or the Food Hygiene Information Scheme (FHIS) in Scotland Data for local authority areas running either of these schemes can be found on the Ratings site: See a list of local authorities running the FHRS or FHIS The scores part of the data is only applicable to scheme type FHRS (not FHIS) and are for hygiene, structure and confidence in management. These scores can be found in part 2 and 3 of Annex 1, A1.1 of the Food Law code of Practice . These scores are then used to calculate the food hygiene rating details of which can be found in the Guidance on implementation and operation of the Food Hygiene Rating Scheme: the Brand Standard and statutory guidance . When a rescore is uploaded by a local authority the scores of hygiene, structure and confidence in management will not be available in the data. Where the establishment is in operation from a private address the address and geocoding data may not be available. The LocalAuthorityBusinessID is provided by the local authority and is unique for that particular local authority data but could also be used by other local authorities. The FHRSID is system-generated and is unique in the data. It is based on the LocalAuthorityBusinessID and the LocalAuthorityCode . Where a new LocalAuthorityBusinessID is uploaded to the system by a local authority, a new FHRSID is generated. If a LocalAuthorityBusinessID is reused, for example for a new registration, the FHRSID will be retained for the establishment. Please note some local authorities use their database as a business database whereas others use an establishment database, therefore some local authorities will recycle the LocalAuthorityBusinessID where others will not. There are circumstances where the LocalAuthorityBusinessID and FHRSID may change, such as local authorities changing databases or where local authorities have merged. Details of where this has occurred can be found on the FHRS status page . Other useful information can be found on this page such as data types for fields. The business types and associated ID's can be found at: api1-ratings.food.gov.uk/business-types/xml Where Awaiting Publication is displayed instead of a rating, this is where the business has appealed their rating, and the local authority is in the process of determining the appeal. NewRatingPending is displayed as true in the data where a local authority has uploaded new data for an establishment which is not yet published as this data is in the notification or appeals period. It will be published after these time periods have elapsed. Where this is displayed as false, no new data is in the workflow to be published. Further information about the scheme can be found at https://www.food.gov.uk/safety-hygiene/food-hygiene-rating-scheme System status Status updates, usage advice and various other pieces of current information can be found at the System Status Page. API guidance for developers The API allows developers access to the underlying food hygiene rating data published at ratings.food.gov.uk . Developers can query XML files to return the geocoded data (longitude and latitude data are provided for food businesses). The XML data are updated daily and can be found below, grouped by local authority. Wales's local authority data can be output in English or Welsh. The API can also be used to query the live system (the data are automatically updated as local authorities upload and publish data) and return data in XML and JSON formats. Examples of how to use the API and information about the API can be found in the guidance document for developers: Read the API V1 guidance for developers (pdf 316KB, updated April 2024) Read the API V2 guidance for developers Images A set of hygiene rating images is available to be used with the API data. The images must only be used in accordance with the FHRS/FHIS Brand Standard and the terms and conditions . Examples of hygiene rating images, and the sizes available, that can be used with the API data: Download new high resolution FHRS badges (ZIP - 1 MB) Legacy online rating images The previous version of the online ratings has now been retired. Please use the images provided above. Score descriptors English language Welsh language Downloading data from the FHRS search results page When you search for hygiene ratings on www.food.gov.uk/ratings , you can download the search results at the bottom of the page. Number of results You can download up to 5,000 results by entering a number between 1 and 5,000 in the 'Number of results' field. If you need to download more than 5,000 results, in the 'Number of results' field enter 5,000, then enter each 'Page number' 1, 2 etc until all results are downloaded. Data formats Data can be downloaded in XML and JSON format. To convert the data into excel format use the following guidance:: Microsoft support page: Open an XML data file to import its data into Excel (Opens in a new tab) To merge multiple Excel files into a single file use the following guidance: Microsoft support page: Import data from a folder with multiple files (Opens in a new tab) Downloadable open data file A complete record of our open food hygiene rating data can be downloaded via the link below. The data is updated daily. You can obtain data for individual regions further down the page, or via the API. articles.title: Rochdale AFC Manager Urges Team to Aim High This Season
articles.excerpt: Rochdale AFC's manager has called on his players to set ambitious goals as they prepare for upcoming matches, emphasising their potential for success in the league.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale AFC's manager has encouraged his players to pursue high aspirations this season. In a recent interview, he expressed confidence in the team's abilities and the importance of setting ambitious goals for their upcoming fixtures.

He highlighted the need for the squad to demonstrate resilience and determination as they face the challenges of the league. The manager believes that with hard work and commitment, the team can achieve significant success.

Fans can expect to see the team striving for excellence in their next matches, as the manager's message resonates throughout the squad. Building momentum and securing vital points will be crucial as the season progresses.

Supporters will be keen to see how the team's performance aligns with the manager's vision in the upcoming fixtures, which are vital for their standing in the league table.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Celebrates Achievements of Over 200 Cared-for Children at Annual Awards
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council hosted its annual awards ceremony at Matthew Moss High School, recognising the achievements of more than 200 cared-for children with medals and a day of entertainment.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council held its annual awards ceremony on 16 October at Matthew Moss High School, celebrating the achievements of over 200 cared-for children. The event, known as 'Our Big Day', recognised the resilience and determination of young people in care, with hundreds of medals awarded to honour their individual successes.

The council received 273 nominations from carers, teachers, and social workers, highlighting the inspiring journeys of children up to the age of 12. Awards were given for exceptional progress in education, sporting achievements, acts of kindness, and positive attitudes in the face of adversity. The day included a variety of entertainment, such as trampolines, funfair rides, and face painting, allowing families to create joyful memories together.

Councillor Rachel Massey, cabinet member for children’s services and education, expressed her pride in the achievements of the children, stating, "They are all exceptional young people and show phenomenal determination to be their very best. This doesn’t go unnoticed by those around them." The event aimed to provide public recognition for the hard work and accomplishments of these young individuals.

Local businesses sponsored the celebration, contributing to the activities and entertainment provided for families. Notable sponsors included A&T Surfacing Ltd, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing, and Rochdale Hornets, among others. This community support helped create a memorable day for the children and their families.

articles.title: St Cuthbert’s RC High School Closes Following Bomb Threat
articles.excerpt: St Cuthbert’s RC High School in Rochdale was evacuated and closed on 16 October after receiving a suspected bomb threat. All students and staff were reported safe, and police are investigating the incident.
articles.content_html:
St Cuthbert’s RC High School in Rochdale was evacuated and closed on Friday morning, 16 October, after staff received a communication regarding a possible bomb threat. The school, located on Shaw Road, implemented emergency procedures to ensure the safety of all students and staff.

In response to the threat, Greater Manchester Police were called to the scene, and the school entered a lockdown as a precautionary measure. A spokesperson for the school confirmed that all children and staff were safe and accounted for during the incident. The police assessed the situation and indicated that the call was likely a hoax.

The St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust, which oversees the school, stated that specialist security operatives would conduct a thorough sweep of the premises to determine if any further action was necessary. Parents and carers were informed that they could collect their children or give permission for them to travel home safely.

The school is expected to reopen as normal on Monday, 19 October, pending the outcome of the police investigation. Authorities have urged the public to refrain from speculation on social media regarding false rumours related to the incident.

articles.title: St Cuthbert’s evacuated as message reassures parents all children and staff are safe
articles.excerpt: St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust says St Cuthbert’s was evacuated following a possible bomb threat. All children and staff are safe; parents can collect pupils.
articles.content_html:
Latest update — St Teresa of Calcutta trust statement

St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust, which oversees St Cuthbert’s RC High School, has released a statement saying staff received a communication detailing a possible bomb threat on Friday morning, 16 October.

The trust says emergency services were called, all school buildings were evacuated as a precaution and Greater Manchester Police attended. All children and staff are safe and accounted for, it says.

Parents and carers can now collect their children or give consent for them to travel home, according to the statement. The trust says specialist security operatives will carry out a full sweep of the building this afternoon. It currently expects the school to reopen as normal on Monday 19 October, subject to further updates.

The trust’s account conflicts with some earlier reports circulating about the incident. In particular, it describes rumours of intruders or weapons on school premises as false. Earlier references to a lockdown should be read alongside this latest statement, which describes a precautionary evacuation following a possible bomb threat.

This remains a developing story. Rochdale Daily will continue to update this article with official information as it is released. The earlier updates below are retained for context; the latest trust statement takes precedence where accounts differ.

Trust statement in full:

Earlier this morning (Friday 16 October 2026), staff at St. Cuthbert's RC High School in Rochdale received a communication detailing a possible bomb threat to the premises.

The emergency services were called and all school buildings were evacuated as a precautionary measure.

All children and staff are safe and accounted for, in line with our established procedures.

Greater Manchester Police attended and parents and carers were notified immediately that their children had been removed to a safe distance and there was no threat or danger to anyone present.

We would like to assure everyone within the St Cuthbert’s School community that the safety and wellbeing of our children remains our absolute priority.

Specialist security operatives will conduct a full sweep of the building this afternoon to confirm if any further actions are required.

Currently, the expectation is that the school will be open as normal on Monday 19 October - but further information will be communicated as needed when received.

Parents and carers can now attend the school to collect their children, or provide consent for their children to travel home.

We’d like to thank parents, carers and colleagues for their understanding and co-operation in this matter.

We’d also urge people to avoid speculation on social media - particularly regarding false rumours, such as any referring to intruders or weapons being present on school premises.

More details will be communicated when appropriate, following consultation with GMP and Rochdale Borough Council.

Source: Statement attributed to St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust, supplied to Rochdale Daily on 16 October 2026.

Earlier updates — before the trust statement

Developing update — councillor requests official briefing

Councillor Jordan Tarrant-Short has said he is urgently requesting an update from Rochdale Council and Greater Manchester Police following reports of a lockdown at Saint Cuthbert’s High School. In a statement supplied to Rochdale Daily, he said he first learned of the reports through the Manchester Evening News and had not received an official briefing.

His statement does not establish what prompted the incident. The earlier message shared with Rochdale Daily described a precautionary evacuation and said all children and staff were safe and accounted for.

Councillor Tarrant-Short’s statement in full:

I want to address the reports of a lockdown at Saint Cuthbert’s High School.

First and foremost, my thoughts are with the children, their families and the staff. I understand how frightening this situation will be, particularly for parents waiting for information and reassurance.

I want to be clear: I first became aware of this through the Manchester Evening News. I have not received an official briefing.

I am now urgently requesting an update from Rochdale Council and Greater Manchester Police so I can understand what has happened and what support is being provided to those affected.

Having been through a similar situation myself when Newhouse Academy went into lockdown, I know how distressing that uncertainty can feel. Behind every update are children who may be frightened and families desperate to know their loved ones are safe.

I am asking that communication with families is timely, clear and compassionate, and that support is available for anyone left distressed.

Until there is verified information, I will not speculate about the circumstances. Please follow official updates from the school and police, and avoid sharing rumours.

The immediate priority must be the safety and wellbeing of every child and member of staff.

Earlier report

St Cuthbert’s RC High School in Rochdale has been evacuated as a precaution, according to a message to parents and carers shared with Rochdale Daily.

The message states: “All children and staff are safe and accounted for.”

It reassures families that pupils’ safety and wellbeing remain the school’s “absolute priority” and says staff are managing the situation in line with established procedures.

Parents and carers have been told they will receive another communication as soon as further information is available.

The message does not explain what prompted the evacuation or give instructions for collecting children.

St Cuthbert’s is on Shaw Road in Rochdale. The school’s website is https://www.stcuthberts.stoccat.org.uk/.

This is a developing story.

Source: Screenshot of a message to parents and carers supplied to Rochdale Daily on Friday 16 October 2026. The screenshot does not display a sender or timestamp; it was identified as St Cuthbert’s by the person who supplied it.

Additional source: Councillor Jordan Tarrant-Short’s statement supplied to Rochdale Daily on 16 October 2026. Councillor name checked against Rochdale Council’s councillor directory.

articles.title: Rochdale Fitness Group to Undertake 100km Arctic Challenge for Cancer Charities
articles.excerpt: Eighteen runners from Resilience gym in Rochdale will embark on a 100km run across the Arctic wilderness on January 29, 2027, to raise funds for cancer charities.
articles.content_html:
A local fitness community in Rochdale is gearing up for a challenging 100-kilometre run across the Arctic wilderness of Swedish Lapland, set to take place on January 29, 2027. The event, known as the Ultra 4 Cancer challenge, will see 18 runners from Resilience gym tackle extreme conditions, including temperatures that may plunge to -30°C, over the course of two days.

The initiative is led by Martin Stapleton, founder and head coach of Resilience gym. Stapleton, a Rochdale-born former Royal Marines Commando and professional MMA fighter, has a history of extreme fundraising efforts, including kayaking the length of the Rochdale Canal and running along the River Thames to support Help for Heroes. Joining him on this expedition are assistant coaches Greg Egan and Oliver Roxburgh, the latter of whom has a personal connection to the cause.

The team aims to raise vital funds for four cancer charities, highlighting the importance of community support in tackling such a significant health issue. The challenge not only tests the physical endurance of the participants but also serves to raise awareness and funds for cancer research and support services.

As the date approaches, the runners will be preparing for the harsh conditions they will face, with training sessions likely to intensify. Community members interested in supporting the cause can follow the team's progress and contribute to their fundraising efforts through the Resilience gym's social media channels.

articles.title: Fireworks distributor with Rochdale premises fined £40,000 as fire service takes enforcement action
articles.excerpt: GMFRS has announced prosecutions over fireworks storage and licensing breaches, including a £40,000 fine for Boom Fireworks, which operates premises in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
A national fireworks distributor operating premises in Rochdale has been fined £40,000 following an investigation by Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service.

GMFRS announced prosecutions involving Boom Fireworks Limited and two Greater Manchester retailers after inspectors uncovered fireworks storage and licensing offences.

According to the fire service, Boom Fireworks operates distribution premises in Cheetham Hill and Rochdale. Its director, Hashum Malik, pleaded guilty to storage offences at Manchester Magistrates’ Court on October 6.

Inspectors discovered higher-risk Hazard Type 3 fireworks being stored contrary to licensing requirements. The stock was detained and removed, and the company received a £40,000 fine, alongside a surcharge and prosecution costs.

Separate cases concerned The Vape Store on Hollins Road in Oldham and Wise Buys on Bury Road in Bolton.

The Oldham shopkeeper received a suspended prison sentence after fireworks were stored and sold despite an expired licence. The Bolton shopkeeper received rehabilitation requirements and a curfew after inspectors found fireworks stored and sold without a valid licence. Courts ordered the seized fireworks destroyed.

What this means for late-night fireworks

For Rochdale residents disturbed by repeated late-night fireworks, the announcement highlights enforcement against businesses supplying and storing explosive products.

However, the prosecutions concern storage and licensing offences. Their effect on fireworks nuisance in individual neighbourhoods has not been established.

The existing rules already prohibit setting off fireworks between 11pm and 7am on most nights. The exceptions are:

Bonfire Night: fireworks may be used until midnight.

New Year’s Eve, Diwali and Chinese New Year: the cut-off is 1am.

Midnight is therefore not the usual permitted finishing time: on ordinary nights, the restriction begins an hour earlier.

How to report persistent problems

Greater Manchester Police says irresponsible fireworks use can harm people and animals, damage property and create a serious fire risk.

Residents experiencing an ongoing problem can report fireworks-related antisocial behaviour through GMP: https://www.gmp.police.uk/advice/advice-and-information/asb/asb/antisocial-behaviour/fireworks/

The force also advises reporting retailers selling adult fireworks to under-18s to Trading Standards.

Sources:

GMFRS prosecution announcement, published 14 October 2026: https://manchesterfire.gov.uk/news/gmfrs-prosecutes-national-fireworks-distributor-and-two-retailers-over-explosives-licensing-breaches/

Government guidance on fireworks rules: https://www.gov.uk/fireworks-the-law

Greater Manchester Police fireworks advice: https://www.gmp.police.uk/advice/advice-and-information/asb/asb/antisocial-behaviour/fireworks/
