articles.title: Safeguarding concerns, community costs and fireworks raised at Rochdale council meeting
articles.excerpt: Farooq Ahmed raised concerns about safeguarding powers, while Jordan Tarrant-Short questioned venue costs, fireworks, foster care and Warwick Mill at full council.
articles.content_html:
Concerns about the potential misuse of safeguarding powers, community venue charges and fireworks nuisance were raised during Rochdale’s full council meeting on Thursday, October 15.

Councillor Farooq Ahmed questioned how the council prevented staff from overstepping their authority, while Councillor Jordan Tarrant-Short pressed cabinet members on issues including foster-carer recruitment, Warwick Mill and access to community facilities.

Councillors also rejected a proposal to rescind the council’s climate emergency commitments and backed motions concerning energy costs in new homes, protecting pubs and condemning attacks on places of worship.

Concern over safeguarding powers

Ahmed stressed that protecting vulnerable adults and children must come first, but questioned whether safeguarding procedures could sometimes harm the people they were intended to protect.

He said some officers could overstep their authority, leaving service users and families feeling victimised. He suggested the term safeguarding could be abused and asked how the council ensured staff did not misuse their powers.

Councillor Shah Wazir said safeguarding should protect and support people without causing avoidable distress. He outlined expectations around involving residents in decisions, providing advocacy where required and reviewing complaints and practice.

Responding to Ahmed’s supplementary question, Wazir invited him to provide specific incidents and promised they would be examined. The mayor also encouraged Ahmed to report his concerns.

The exchange raised concerns about potential misuse; it did not establish that misconduct had occurred in any particular case.

Community groups facing venue costs

Tarrant-Short said community organisations had contacted him about hire charges at facilities managed by Your Trust, warning that costs could make their activities financially unsustainable.

He told the meeting that a local dance group had reported being quoted £11,000 for one evening at Heywood Civic Centre. The booking requirements and an explanation of that reported quotation were not established during the exchange.

He asked whether protections, concessions or community pricing policies could prevent voluntary organisations being priced out.

Councillor Sue Smith said reduced rates or room-hire waivers could be available where appropriate, but charges also had to cover staffing, technical support and other operating costs.

She asked him to send details so officers could investigate. Smith said she had helped groups reduce charges, sometimes through changes to booking dates or times, but did not announce a new borough-wide pricing policy.

Fireworks and stronger safeguards

Tarrant-Short raised residents’ concerns about fireworks being used throughout the year, describing distress to families, vulnerable people and pets.

He asked what action the council and partner agencies were taking, then pressed for lobbying for stronger regulation and enforcement powers.

Councillor Tricia Ayrton acknowledged the concerns and said she had been speaking with partner agencies about a coordinated response.

She also said the council’s three community bonfire events would use reduced-noise fireworks, accompanied by music and lights. In response to his request for stronger national action, she encouraged councillors to raise concerns with their MPs.

Recruiting and retaining foster carers

Tarrant-Short asked how the council would increase the number of local foster carers and provide enough family placements for vulnerable children.

Councillor Rachel Massey outlined work through the Greater Manchester fostering recruitment hub, alongside specialist fostering, training and support. She identified particular needs for carers supporting teenagers, sibling groups and children with disabilities.

In a supplementary question, Tarrant-Short congratulated the children’s services team before asking what recruitment targets would replace retiring carers and increase overall capacity.

Massey said recruitment strategies and targets existed, while stressing the importance of finding the right home for each child. She did not give a numerical recruitment target in that exchange.

Warwick Mill and local investment

Tarrant-Short asked whether Warwick Mill would be acquired through compulsory purchase.

Council leader Neil Emmott said the council had negotiated an agreement with the owner and that cabinet had approved exercising an option to purchase following due diligence.

Asked why decisive intervention had taken so long, Emmott pointed to private ownership and previous unsuccessful redevelopment proposals, saying the council was now taking action.

Tarrant-Short also called for more community events in Rochdale South, including his Balderstone and Kirkholt ward.

Later, he asked whether a previously discussed highways review meeting had taken place. Scrutiny chair Councillor Tom Besford said no date had yet been arranged and promised to follow it up with him.

Pub protections and council votes

Tarrant-Short formally moved an amendment to the pub-protection motion, which councillors approved unanimously. The amended motion subsequently passed, supporting action over restrictive covenants that can prevent former pubs reopening.

Councillors unanimously supported motions on reducing energy costs in new homes and condemning attacks on places of worship.

A proposal to rescind the council’s climate emergency commitments was defeated.

Source: Rochdale Borough Council full council webcast, 15 October 2026: https://rochdale.public-i.tv/core/portal/webcast_interactive/1133238

articles.title: Future of College Bank Towers Uncertain as Renovation Could Take Over a Decade
articles.excerpt: Housing chiefs have stated that renovating the College Bank tower blocks would displace residents for more than ten years, with no decision yet made on their future.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) has confirmed that no decision has been made regarding the future of the College Bank tower blocks, known locally as the Seven Sisters. However, housing officials have warned that any renovation of the iconic structures would require residents to vacate their homes for over a decade.

The Seven Sisters, which have stood for 61 years, are in urgent need of modernisation. Residents have been advocating for refurbishment rather than demolition, and recently appealed to Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig for support in their campaign. If the renovation proceeds, RBH has indicated that the buildings would not be habitable until the extensive work is completed.

The discussion around the future of College Bank began in 2017 when RBH expressed concerns about the buildings nearing the end of their lifespan. In response, tenants formed the Save the Seven Sisters campaign, hoping that a partnership with Legal and General Affordable Homes would lead to restoration. However, in September 2024, it was announced that this partnership would not continue, prompting further calls for assistance from local leaders.

In November 2024, a Mayoral Taskforce was established to explore options for the College Bank estate. Following safety surveys conducted in October 2025, RBH declared that the blocks were unsafe for occupancy, necessitating the relocation of residents. As the situation develops, the community awaits clarity on the next steps for the future of their homes.

evidence_sources.captured_text: No decision yet on College Bank – but ‘renovation would take more than a decade’ - Rochdale Times Skip to content LATEST NEWS No decision yet on College Bank – but ‘renovation would take more than a decade’ Renovating Rochdale’s iconic Seven Sisters tower blocks would force residents out of their homes for more than a decade, housing chiefs have said. While Rochdale Boroughwide Housing says no decision on the future of the landmark College Bank blocks has been taken, residents have asked new Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig to back their campaign to refurbish their homes rather than demolish them. But if campaigners get their wish, the scale of bringing the 61-year-old buildings up to modern standards would take more than 10 years and they could not be occupied until the work is complete, RBH chiefs have said. Members of Greater Manchester Tenants Union recently met Ms Craig to discuss the steps that could be taken to renovate almost 1,000 homes in College Bank and Lower Falinge. Plans to demolish College Bank were first discussed in 2017 when RBH warned that the buildings were approaching the end of their life. Tenants set up the Save the Seven Sisters campaign and hoped RBH’s partnership with Legal and General Affordable Homes would see the towers restored. But in September, 2024, it was announced that the partnership would not continue. The union and the Save the Seven Sisters campaign asked then Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham to help. In November, 2024, the Mayoral Taskforce was established to look at the options for the College Bank estate. Rochdale’s skyline without the Seven Sisters towers. Image: Copilot In October 2025, RBH announced the results of surveys which found the blocks were not safe to remain occupied and residents would be required to leave their homes. Campaigners refute the claims and have used Freedom of Information Act requests for Building Safety Regulator documents relating to College Bank and Lower Falinge. The tenants union said: “It is clear from these documents and statements that for the past two years RBH has been unable or unwilling to comply with the Building Safety Regulator’s requirements for an action plan to address issues which need to be resolved in the medium term at College Bank. “This includes straightforward basic repairs, cyclical maintenance and issues that would be addressed in any refurbishment plan.” While RBH says no decision on the future of the College Bank tower blocks has been taken, campaigners want the demolition of Lower Falinge properties to stop. The landmark College Bank tower blocks dominate Rochdale’s skyline The tenants union said: “None of the Lower Falinge residents the campaigners have spoken to want this demolition to go ahead, not least because it will decimate the beautiful urban greenspace and considerable biodiversity in the town centre estate. “RBH refuses to explain why refurbishment is considered too expensive an option. Instead it prefers to continually make unfounded assertions that the homes in Lower Falinge are ‘end-of-life’, that they ‘cannot be occupied’, and that they mysteriously can ‘no longer provide safe, warm homes’ for residents. “Residents on both estates can see that RBH has deliberately created unfit and unsafe homes through managed decline of housing that they were entrusted with when all the council’s housing was transferred to it in early 2012.” College Bank resident Ann Jones said: “At a consultation workshop in 2017, one of RBH’s architects was attempting to steer me towards choosing the option for College Bank which involved demolition. READ MORE: Police officer sentenced for injuring pedestrian in high-speed crash Vacant blocks on the Lower Falinge estate. Image: Google “This was their aim back then. Today, citing the structural surveys whilst withholding their content, to get people out, is the latest device to try and achieve the demolition of over 750 homes on College Bank alone, while they also intend to demolish over 140 homes on Lower Falinge. This is completely unacceptable in a housing crisis.” Lower Falinge tenant Andrew Roche said: “I love living on Falinge, and the prospect of losing my home to RBH’s bulldozers is devastating.” Rochdale MP Paul Waugh backed calls for a swift resolution. He said: “Tenants have been left in limbo for far too long and I hope that they can be given the answers they need about the safety and the future of their homes. “I urge RBH to act as swiftly as possible to bring this to a conclusion on behalf of all Rochdale residents during a housing emergency. “Each day these flats are left empty is another missed opportunity to support the many thousands of Rochdalians living in temporary or unsuitable accommodation. “The council and GMCA have confirmed their commitment to resolving this longstanding and emotive issue, and I will continue to work with colleagues across government to ensure the best quality housing in Rochdale is realised.” Rochdale MP Paul Waugh Hannah Fleming, Director of Regeneration and Asset Improvement at Rochdale Boroughwide Housing, said: “It’s important that we make the right decision on the future of College Bank. “Our focus throughout has been on doing the right thing for current and future customers, ensuring we can provide safe, warm, affordable homes that meet housing need for generations to come. “Future regeneration options are still being discussed with our partners, including Rochdale Council and the Mayor of Greater Manchester. No final decision has yet been made by the RBH Board. “What we do know is that there are no simple options. The buildings are more than 60 years old and have continued to deteriorate. Keeping them would require very major works requiring customers to move out for at least a decade. “That is why, in October, 2025, the board made the difficult decision to begin rehousing customers while longer-term plans are considered. This decision was taken because of concerns about the long-term condition and safety of the buildings, and not because any final regeneration decision had been reached. “We have already made significant progress on the rehousing programme, with just under 90 households left to find their new home and most customers already settled in their new homes. “We are working individually with each household to ensure their move is as simple and straightforward as it possibly can be.” The mayor’s office has been approached for a comment. articles.title: Inclusive roundabout and zip line feature in plans for new Falinge Park play area
articles.excerpt: Mayoress Iram Faisal has unveiled plans for new play equipment at Falinge Park, including a wheelchair-accessible roundabout, an inclusive seesaw and a double cableway zip line.
articles.content_html:
Plans for a new play area at Falinge Park have been unveiled, with wheelchair-accessible equipment among the attractions proposed for children and families.

Mayoress Iram Faisal shared details of the project, describing it as a deeply personal undertaking in the park where she played as a child.

The proposed equipment includes a double cableway zip line with ramps; a toddler multi-play unit; toddler and junior swings; an inclusive seesaw; a Crazy Gander springer; and a wheelchair-accessible roundabout.

In her announcement, Mrs Faisal said inclusivity had been central to the vision, with the aim of helping more children enjoy the park together.

“Every child deserves the opportunity to play, explore and enjoy their childhood,” she said.

For the Mayoress, the plans also carry memories of her own upbringing.

“Having lived here and played in this very park myself, to now be in a position to play a part in transforming it for the next generation has been an incredibly emotional journey,” she said.

She thanked councillors Faisal Rana and Amber Nisa, Rochdale Borough Council and its Environmental Management Team, alongside everyone involved in bringing the project forward.

Mrs Faisal said the improvements were about investing in children and creating a space where families could make memories together.

“From playing in Falinge Park as a child to helping shape its future, this really is a full-circle moment,” she added.

The announcement refers to a hoped-for start towards the end of February, with work continuing into March, subject to final arrangements. It does not specify the year or confirm an opening date, so that timetable remains to be clarified.

Residents have been invited to share their views on the proposals.

Source: announcement by Mayoress Iram Faisal, supplied to Rochdale Daily and published on her public Facebook page: https://www.facebook.com/iram.faisal.5095/posts/1764829918060894/

articles.title: Emmerdale star Lisa Riley meets shoppers as Peacocks opens in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Peacocks opened its new Rochdale Riverside store on Thursday, with Emmerdale star Lisa Riley joining the celebrations and posing for photographs with shoppers.
articles.content_html:
Peacocks opened its new Rochdale Riverside store today, with Emmerdale star Lisa Riley joining the celebrations and posing for photographs with shoppers.

The actress helped officially launch the branch on Thursday 15 October, cutting the ribbon alongside store manager Claire Kershaw and the shop team. Riley also celebrated the visit on her own social media, confirming she had opened the new store.

Her appearance gave shoppers an opportunity to meet a familiar television face while exploring the retailer’s latest addition to Rochdale town centre.

Customers were keen to get through the doors, with the first shopper reportedly arriving at 6.30am. The first ten customers each received a £50 Peacocks gift card.

The new branch stocks clothing for women, men and children, bringing Peacocks back to the town following the closure of its former Wheatsheaf Shopping Centre shop in 2020.

For residents pleased to see the name return, today was a chance to browse the new shop, meet its staff and enjoy a little soap-star glamour alongside their shopping.

Sources: Roch Valley Radio’s opening-day report: https://www.rochvalleyradio.com/news-features/140/business/1040/lisa-riley-opens-new-peacocks-store-at-rochdale-riverside Lisa Riley’s public opening announcement: https://www.facebook.com/officiallisariley/posts/1657501805737969/ Shoppers’ photographs: information supplied to Rochdale Daily.

articles.title: Rochdale’s Owen Webster ready for fresh start in BKFC featherweight clash
articles.excerpt: Rochdale-born Owen Webster says he is ready to “take over the game” ahead of his featherweight bout against Dan Morel at Glasgow’s OVO Hydro on 7 November.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale-born Owen Webster says he is ready to “take over the game” as he prepares to return to Bare Knuckle Fighting Championship in a new weight class.

Webster is scheduled to face Dan Morel in a featherweight bout at BKFC 96 at Glasgow’s OVO Hydro on Saturday 7 November. The contest is listed on the promotion’s official fight card.

Looking ahead to his return, Webster told supporters: “3 Weeks on Saturday and I make that walk again, totally different fighter whole new weight class but still ready to take over the game.”

His message signals confidence ahead of a change in division, with Webster promising supporters a different version of himself when he steps back into the ring.

For the Rochdale fighter, the Glasgow appearance offers an opportunity to make his mark at featherweight and begin a fresh chapter in his BKFC career.

Morel stands between him and that ambition. BKFC’s official profile lists Morel as a featherweight with a promotional record of no wins, losses or draws ahead of their meeting.

The event marks BKFC’s Scottish debut and is headlined by Conor Cooke defending the UK light heavyweight championship against Sean Weir. Webster’s contest is a featherweight matchup on the card; it is not listed as a title fight.

Supporters can find ticket and viewing information through the official BKFC event page: https://www.bkfc.com/events/bkfc-glasgow

With a new weight class and a determined message to his rivals, Webster will be looking to give his hometown something to celebrate on 7 November.

Sources: Owen Webster’s statement supplied to Rochdale Daily; BKFC’s official event listing and Dan Morel fighter profile; venue event details: https://www.sec.co.uk/events/detail/bare-knuckle-fighting-championship

articles.title: Rochdale social worker Nneamaka Uti shortlisted for national award
articles.excerpt: Nneamaka Uti, who works in Rochdale Council’s adult care service, is a finalist in the Social Worker of the Year Awards, with winners announced on 22 October.
articles.content_html:
A social worker helping adults in Rochdale has been shortlisted for a national award recognising outstanding work in the profession.

Nneamaka Uti, who works in Rochdale Borough Council’s adult care service, is a finalist for Newly Qualified Adult Social Worker of the Year at the 2026 Social Worker of the Year Awards.

The winners will be announced on Thursday 22 October, at an awards reception in London. The organisers have confirmed that the afternoon event will run from 2pm to 5pm.

Councillor Shah Wazir, the council’s cabinet member for adult care, welcomed the recognition.

He said: “This is lovely and deserved recognition for Nneamaka and showcases Rochdale’s caring side at its very best. Following adult care’s good CQC rating this underlines the high-quality care and support the council is delivering for residents across the borough. Best of luck to Nneamaka at the awards ceremony.”

The council’s announcement links Nneamaka’s shortlisting with the adult care service’s good Care Quality Commission rating, highlighting the contribution of staff supporting residents across the borough.

Now marking their 20th anniversary, the Social Worker of the Year Awards recognise achievements across children’s and adult social work in England. This year, the organisers have named 64 finalists across 14 categories.

Nneamaka is one of six finalists in the newly qualified adult social worker category. The shortlist recognises practitioners at the beginning of their careers, giving Rochdale a representative among those in contention for national recognition.

Gold and silver award recipients will be announced at the October reception.

Rochdale Daily wishes Nneamaka the best of luck.

Sources: Rochdale Borough Council announcement supplied to Rochdale Daily; official shortlist: https://www.socialworkawards.com/news/social-worker-of-the-year-award-finalists-announced-2026/ Event details: https://www.socialworkawards.com/awards-night/award-faqs/

articles.title: Rochdale Council Announces Free Bonfire Night Events for November 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council will host three free firework displays across the borough in early November, featuring reduced noise fireworks for accessibility.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has confirmed a series of free firework displays to celebrate Bonfire Night in November 2026. The events will take place at three locations across the borough, including Middleton, Heywood, and Syke, with festivities beginning on Monday, November 2.

The first event will be held at Bowlee Community Park, located on Heywood Old Road in Middleton, starting at 6pm. The bonfire will be lit at 7pm, followed by fireworks at 7.30pm. The second display will occur on Tuesday, November 3, at Queen’s Park Road in Heywood, with the same timings. The final council-run event will take place on Wednesday, November 4, at Cronkeyshaw Common in Syke, also starting at 6pm.

In addition to the council events, Milnrow Cricket Club and Lobden Golf Club in Whitworth will host their own firework displays on Saturday, November 7. The Milnrow event will charge £7 for adults and £11.25 for families, while the Lobden Golf Club display will cost £5 for adults and £3 for children.

Rochdale Council has introduced reduced noise fireworks this year to make the displays more accessible for all attendees. The council advises visitors to walk or use public transport due to limited parking at the venues. Alcohol, fireworks, and sparklers are prohibited at all council-run events, and no toilet facilities will be available.

The council confirms the Rochdale display is on Wednesday 4 November 2026: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/481/rochdale-bonfire-and-fireworks-display

Original source: https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/whats-on/family-kids-news/rochdale-bonfire-night-2026-firework-34765383

articles.title: Ofsted Inspection Report Published for Little Wonders Nursery in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Ofsted has released a new inspection report for Little Wonders Nursery, detailing its findings and the rating awarded following the recent assessment.
articles.content_html:
Ofsted has published a new inspection report for Little Wonders Nursery, located in Rochdale. The report, dated 15 October 2026, outlines the findings from the recent inspection and includes the rating awarded to the nursery.

Settings registered on the Early Years Register are typically inspected at least once within a four-year period. However, Ofsted prioritises inspections and may conduct them more frequently if there are concerns. Newly registered settings are inspected within 18 months of their registration date.

The report provides insights into the quality of care and education provided at Little Wonders Nursery, which is essential for parents considering childcare options in the area. Parents can access the full report on the Ofsted website for detailed information regarding the nursery's performance and any areas for improvement.

For those interested in the nursery or similar childcare providers, Ofsted encourages parents to search and compare other pre-school and day nursery options nearby. Additionally, parents can subscribe to alerts to be notified when new reports are published for this provider.

Nantwich Town Women advanced to the next round of the Women’s FA Cup following a 3-1 victory against Rochdale AFC at the Crown Oil Arena on October 15. The Dabbers dominated the match, creating numerous chances and controlling possession throughout.

Nantwich goalkeeper Connie was instrumental in the win, making several key saves to keep Rochdale at bay. The visitors took an early lead and maintained pressure on the home side, who struggled to find their rhythm.

Despite a spirited effort from Rochdale, they could only manage one goal in response to Nantwich's three. The defeat means Rochdale will now focus on their league fixtures as they look to bounce back from this cup exit.

The result highlights Nantwich's strong form in the competition and sets them up for a promising next round.

articles.title: Halloween in Rochdale 2026: parties, pumpkins and spooky events across the borough
articles.excerpt: 39 dated Halloween listings across Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Milnrow, Littleborough, Norden and Wardle, with prices, times, age suitability, venues and booking links.
articles.content_html:
From free family fun at the Town Hall and Empire to pool parties, pumpkin carving, costume competitions and late-night entertainment, here is our area-by-area guide to the spooky season.

Halloween falls on Saturday 31 October this year, but celebrations stretch across half-term and into Sunday 1 November. There are options for young children, teenagers, families and adults, including events advertised on local Facebook pages.

Find your area below. Listings run in date order within each area; events with several dates appear at their first date. Prices are the published figures available when checked. Where hours, age limits, admission charges or booking details remain unconfirmed, we say so.

This guide brings together the public 2026 announcements we could identify and check. Private groups, unadvertised parties and later announcements mean no guide can guarantee every event. Organisers can send additions to news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

Find a plan quickly

Free family events: Town Hall, 26 October–1 November; Empire children’s party, 27 October.

Children’s parties: Rochdale RUFC, Milnrow and Littleborough cricket clubs, BizzyBees and Wardle Club. Check the age policies below.

Older children and teenagers: Younique Talent ages 7–17; Hollingworth Lake activity morning ages 8+; Monsters of Rock for accompanied ages 14+.

A party with a quiet room: Keeley B at Butterworth Hall on 30 October.

Adults: Norden workshops, Royal Toby bingo, Town Hall horror cinema and evening live music. Decadance is separately marked as an adults-only lifestyle venue.

Rochdale town centre

26 October–1 November, daily 10am–4pm

Spooktacular Half Term at Rochdale Town Hall

| Where: Rochdale Town Hall, The Esplanade, OL16 1AZ | Who it’s for: Families | Cost: Free

Organiser’s Facebook announcement → — https://www.facebook.com/empirerochdale/videos/1092430556500653/

Venue event calendar → — https://empirerochdale.co.uk/events/

| Where: Champness Hall, Drake Street, OL16 1NZ | Who it’s for: Adults; ages 14+ may attend with an adult using the appropriate ticket | Cost: Adult £22 including fee; 1 adult + 1 child aged 14+ £33; 1 adult + 2 children aged 14+ £44

Thunder Hammer perform rock and metal tributes, with Halloween fancy dress encouraged. Predominantly standing. The page’s schedule also displays a 7.30pm event start; use the organiser’s 7pm doors guidance and check final timings. Accompanied children and adults must arrive together.

Choose a session and book → — https://www.gardenofedenrochdale.co.uk/design-20179618/childrens-halloween-flowercraft-workshop-31st-oct-2026.htm

Bingo, dance-offs, games, rave intervals and prizes. Tickets include entry, a goody bag and all bingo games; the listing does not say that drinks are included. Direct booking on 01706 861861 or royaltobyfunctions@thedeckersgroup.com is advertised as avoiding booking fees.

Monday 26–Friday 30 October; daily hours not confirmed

Halloween Hair & Horror Club

Younique Talent advertises witches and wizards, zombies, pumpkins, Halloween glam and a Friday showcase. Activities include hair, barbering, media make-up, nails, arts, photography and fitness. Saturday 31 October, from 8pm; finish not stated

| Where: Decadance, 122 Durham Street, Rochdale, OL11 1LS | Who it’s for: Adults 18+ only; adult lifestyle / swingers venue | Cost: Confirm Halloween admission directly; the club announces new standard pricing from 23 October

Rocky Horror-themed fancy dress, dancing, games and costume prizes at an adult lifestyle club. Read the venue’s entry rules before attending. The organiser says advance notice is helpful but visitors can also turn up; admission conditions apply.

Organiser’s event and entry information → — https://www.decadanceswingersclub.com/what-s-on-at-decadance/events-coming-soon/31-10-rocky-horror-halloween-party

Before you book

Check availability and the final checkout total. “From” prices may not cover every ticket type, adult accompaniment or transaction fee. Free entry does not necessarily include food, drinks or optional activities.

Ask organisers about allergies, accessible entrances, toilets, parking, seating and essential-carer admission where these are not specified. Swimming events have their own supervision rules. A quiet room at a busy party does not mean the whole event is a low-sensory session.

Already happened this month

Halloween Horrorfest, Heywood Civic — Saturday 10 October, 10am–5pm. The family-friendly event advertised traders, ghost stories, scare actors and interactive activities. It has already taken place and is not an upcoming booking option. Original event listing — https://stayhappening.com/e/halloween-horrorfest-E2ISYPVLD9D.

More announcements being checked

Rochdale Riverside and The Beach in Littleborough have Halloween promotional pages, but a sufficiently detailed current 2026 programme was not established from the material checked. Old dates have not been reused. Riverside updates — https://rochdaleriverside.com/news/spooktacular-halloween-fun/ · The Beach Halloween page — https://www.greeneking.co.uk/pubs/lancashire/beach/halloween.

An area without its own listing does not mean nothing is happening there. Further dated public announcements can be added as they are verified.

Help keep the guide useful

Running a Halloween event in the borough? Send the date, start and finish times, full venue, age suitability, prices, accessibility details and booking link to news@rochdaledaily.co.uk. Readers: tell us which event you are heading to and share your recommendations.

Sources: Linked organiser websites, venue calendars, ticket pages and public Facebook announcements, including flyers inspected directly. Details and availability checked 15 October 2026. Historical listings and events in similarly named places outside the borough have been excluded.

articles.title: A kitchen to be proud of this Christmas: meet Rochdale’s family-run SJF Granite & Quartz
articles.excerpt: With 25 years of experience and a reported 124 five-star reviews, this local family business puts craftsmanship and personal service at the heart of its work.
articles.content_html:
With 25 years of experience and a reported 124 five-star reviews, this local family business puts craftsmanship and personal service at the heart of its work.

Christmas has a way of bringing everyone into the kitchen. From preparing the festive dinner to catching up over a drink, it becomes the busiest—and often happiest—room in the house.

For anyone dreaming of giving that space a beautiful new finish, Rochdale’s SJF Granite & Quartz Ltd offers local expertise with a personal touch.

The family-owned business specialises in bespoke granite and quartz surfaces, serving homes and businesses across Rochdale, Greater Manchester and surrounding areas. Its website highlights 25 years of experience and a commitment to quality, precision and value for money.

Behind every attractive worktop is careful workmanship. SJF describes a process that takes projects from detailed measurement and templating through to cutting, polishing and installation—bringing the individual elements together into a finished surface tailored to the space.

The reported tally of 124 five-star reviews adds an encouraging chapter to this local family-business story. Choosing someone to work in your home is a matter of trust, and recommendations from previous customers can be an important part of that decision.

SJF places personal service at the centre of its approach, alongside carefully crafted stone and competitive pricing. It is a combination with clear appeal for homeowners who want their kitchen to feel special while keeping their budget in mind.

With Christmas approaching, now is a good time to start discussing the kitchen you have been imagining. Choosing a surface, exploring samples and arranging measurements early gives you time to consider the details and ask about installation availability before the festive season.

Whether your plans involve a complete kitchen renovation or replacing existing worktops, a beautifully chosen surface can become the detail that brings the room together.

SJF’s showroom at 47 Church Street, Littleborough, OL15 8AB offers the opportunity to explore samples. Its website also showcases completed projects and provides a free quotation enquiry form.

For inspiration, project enquiries and Christmas availability, visit https://sjfgraniteandquartz.co.uk/ or call 07311 133375.

Your dream kitchen could start with a conversation—and a family business right here in the Rochdale borough.

articles.title: QTS Group Hosts First Safety Jamboree in Rochdale with Over 350 Attendees
articles.excerpt: The QTS Group's inaugural safety Jamboree at Ashworth Valley Scout Camp in Rochdale attracted more than 350 participants, focusing on health, safety, and innovation in the rail industry.
articles.content_html:
National rail contractor QTS Group hosted its first safety-focused Jamboree at Ashworth Valley Scout Camp in Rochdale, bringing together over 350 colleagues, supply chain partners, and activity hosts. The two-day event, which took place recently, was designed to promote health, safety, and innovation within the rail industry through interactive demonstrations and hands-on activities.

Attendees had the opportunity to engage with new technology and best practices from various suppliers and specialists. Jamie Marks, HSQE Manager at QTS Group, stated that the event aimed to foster knowledge sharing and strengthen relationships across the industry. He noted the positive feedback received and expressed enthusiasm for making next year's event even larger and more impactful.

Demonstrations included the Elios 3 drone for aerial mapping, virtual reality experiences simulating drone flights, and a confined space training simulator provided by Eurosafe. Participants also tested their skills on an excavator simulator from Flannery Plant Hire and witnessed mock aerial rescue demonstrations conducted by IRATA-trained teams.

The event not only highlighted the importance of safety in the rail sector but also provided a platform for networking and collaboration among industry professionals. QTS Group plans to build on this success for future events, aiming to further enhance safety practices in the rail industry.

articles.title: Temporary Closure of Hillcrest Road in Rochdale for Roadworks from 26 October 2026
articles.excerpt: Temporary closure of Hillcrest Road will take place from 26 October to 30 October 2026, affecting local traffic and access.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced that Hillcrest Road will be temporarily closed for roadworks from 12 midnight on Monday, 26 October 2026, until 11.59pm on Friday, 30 October 2026. The closure will affect a section of the road, specifically from a point 57 metres east of its junction with Queensway for a distance of 20 metres heading east.

During this period, motorists will need to use alternative routes. The suggested diversion will take drivers along Queensway, Albion Street, and Newchurch Street to navigate around the closure.

This roadworks initiative is part of ongoing efforts by the council to improve local infrastructure and ensure safer travel for residents and visitors. The exact nature of the works has not been detailed in the announcement, but such projects typically involve repairs or upgrades to the road surface and associated facilities.

Local residents and commuters are advised to plan their journeys accordingly and allow for extra travel time during the roadworks. Further updates may be provided as the work progresses, and residents can check the council's website for additional information and maps of the affected areas.

articles.title: College Bank’s future remains a housing question as residents move from the Seven Sisters
articles.excerpt: College Bank’s future cannot yet be presented as a confirmed number of new homes. RBH’s July 2026 update records that 100 customers had accepted offers of another home and 64 had moved from the high-rise blocks at that point.
articles.content_html:
College Bank’s future cannot yet be presented as a confirmed number of new homes. RBH’s July 2026 update records that 100 customers had accepted offers of another home and 64 had moved from the high-rise blocks at that point.

That is evidence of rehousing progress at a particular date, not evidence that replacement homes have been constructed or that a final demolition or refurbishment programme is approved. Earlier reporting described continuing uncertainty over the solution for the Seven Sisters.

RBH says resident safety drives the move and that it is supporting tenants through the process. A complete account should include the position of residents who wish to stay, the available alternatives and any future right-to-return arrangements.

This is separate from the neighbouring Lower Falinge proposal. Combining the two without checking their boundaries and replacement totals risks overstating supply and obscuring the number of existing affordable homes temporarily or permanently lost.

The January 2026 regulator judgement recognises RBH’s governance improvement but identifies material risks around investment and regeneration. It is not a project approval or an assessment of whether demolition is the best option.

Until the final scheme is evidenced, its contribution to the housing target is unknown. The practical questions are the cost, safety and quality of the eventual homes, and whether existing residents benefit from the change.

Location: College Bank / Seven Sisters, Rochdale

Planning stage: Rehousing underway; a verified final replacement or refurbishment scheme not established

Homes: No reliable new-home total established for a final future scheme

Let or for sale: Existing social housing; future tenure and costs require a confirmed scheme

Land: Existing urban residential land

Final planning agreement: No final replacement/refurbishment scheme, permission or executed development agreement was established from the reviewed records.

Exact rents / prices: Exact future rents, service charges and any guaranteed return-tenancy costs cannot be reported without a confirmed scheme and terms. They are not provided in the public update reviewed.

Affordable breakdown: Existing social housing; final retained, demolished and replacement totals, tenure and net gain are not established.

Funded school capacity: No scheme-specific funded capacity established. A final scheme and net household change are needed before assessing additional school demand.

Funded healthcare capacity: No final scheme-specific funded NHS capacity established; rehousing progress does not measure GP capacity.

Funded transport capacity: No final funded transport-capacity package established. Existing town-centre access is not evidence of additional service provision.

The outstanding details identified above are not yet available to Rochdale Daily. This article will be updated when the information becomes available.

Research checked 14 October 2026. Advertised prices are snapshots, not achieved sale prices.

articles.title: Lower Falinge’s proposed 270 homes would replace 150: what residents gain and lose
articles.excerpt: RBH’s next Lower Falinge phase is reported to envisage 270 affordable-rented homes across two parcels, replacing 150 homes proposed for demolition. If implemented on that basis, the eventual net addition is around 120 homes, not 270.
articles.content_html:
RBH’s next Lower Falinge phase is reported to envisage 270 affordable-rented homes across two parcels, replacing 150 homes proposed for demolition. If implemented on that basis, the eventual net addition is around 120 homes, not 270.

The screening-stage proposal includes houses and apartments. It does not itself grant planning permission for the development. The current reference identified in reporting is OTH/2026/0781; final layouts and consent remain separate steps.

There is a directly relevant legal history. Claimants’ barristers reported that the council conceded a challenge to its earlier demolition prior approval over its EIA reasoning. The later October 2025 decision was reported as a refusal. This concerned the decision-making process and should not be recast as a finding of criminal misconduct by a builder.

RBH says regeneration is intended to create safe, warm family homes and has held resident consultation. Existing residents need clear rehousing commitments, costs and any opportunity to return. A temporary loss of homes before replacement is also important for borough-wide supply.

The regulator’s January 2026 judgement confirmed RBH’s G2 governance and V2 viability grades, recognising improvement while identifying risks. It did not assess consumer standards through that stability check.

The infrastructure test must consider the whole regeneration programme and its phases, including services during demolition and reconstruction, rather than treating every parcel as unrelated.

Location: Lower Falinge, north of Rochdale town centre

Planning stage: Regeneration proposals and EIA screening request; full scheme approval not established

Homes: 270 proposed replacement homes; 150 proposed demolitions; about 120 eventual net gain

Let or for sale: Affordable rent proposed; not automatically social rent

Land: Existing housing estate and previously developed urban parcels

Final planning agreement: The new 270-home proposal is at screening/proposal stage in the reviewed records; a final permission and executed agreement were not established. Earlier demolition litigation does not grant approval to this scheme.

Exact rents / prices: Exact new rents, service charges, temporary rehousing costs and return-tenancy terms are not provided in the reviewed council/government records or established from the public proposal.

Affordable breakdown: 270 affordable-rented replacements proposed, not necessarily Social Rent. Demolishing 150 gives about 120 eventual net additions. Bedroom/tenure distribution and binding return rights remain unverified.

Funded school capacity: No scheme-specific funded additional school places, named capital project and opening date were established from the accessible official records reviewed.

Funded healthcare capacity: No site-specific funded NHS expansion, additional staffed appointment capacity or delivery date was established from the accessible council/government records reviewed. Proximity to a surgery is not a capacity assessment.

Funded transport capacity: No funded new transport-service capacity or complete construction-phase access plan established. Services for existing residents also matter during rehousing and demolition.

The outstanding details identified above are not yet available to Rochdale Daily. This article will be updated when the information becomes available.

Research checked 14 October 2026. Advertised prices are snapshots, not achieved sale prices.

articles.title: Where Rochdale’s next homes are planned—and who can afford them
articles.excerpt: Our investigation examines 22 housing developments and regeneration plans across Rochdale borough: homes, prices, affordable tenure, land, school places, GP capacity and transport funding.
articles.content_html:
The homes are planned, but will Rochdale get the housing its residents need?

Rochdale’s housing pipeline spans large farmland neighbourhoods, former industrial and retail sites, and replacement of existing social housing. The schemes are at different stages. Allocated land, a committee resolution, a formal permission, a construction start and an occupied home are not interchangeable.

How many homes is Rochdale expected to deliver?

The council’s 2026 housing topic paper uses the adopted Places for Everyone requirement of 10,472 net additional homes in 2022–2039: 568 annually in 2022–2025, 616 in 2025–2030 and 632 in 2030–2039. It records 650 net additions in 2024/25, above that year’s 568 requirement. This is historical performance, not proof of delivery in 2026/27.

Does the pipeline meet the government’s target?

The answer is qualified. The 2025 land assessment identifies sufficient potential supply against the adopted plan benchmark, but availability forecasts do not guarantee completions. National housing need is a separate calculation, using housing stock and affordability. The current national framework was issued in August 2026; older council estimates of the revised need are not interchangeable with a freshly calculated October figure. The latest annual delivery, current standard-method calculation and appropriate land-supply buffer still need confirmation before claiming the borough meets every present national requirement.

Why affordable numbers matter

The May 2026 housing-needs assessment estimates a net annual affordable shortfall of 768 homes under a ten-year backlog-clearance model. That is an assessment of need, not a separate statutory annual building quota, and includes the role of existing stock. Appendix C contains the detailed calculation; its headline gross figures are internally inconsistent, so this series uses the consistent net figure. The distinction is essential: meeting an overall housing target does not automatically meet the needs of households who cannot afford market homes.

What does affordable mean?

Social Rent is set under government rent policy. Other affordable rental products are regulated or discounted against local rents. Shared ownership and discounted sale help eligible purchasers but still involve household costs. For each scheme, actual rent, purchase price, unowned-share rent, service charges, estate fees and eligibility are the useful affordability evidence. A marketing incentive or a claim that a property is cheaper than Manchester does not establish planning-defined affordability.

Green Belt and brownfield are different questions

Green Belt is a planning designation; greenfield and brownfield describe the land and its development history. Agricultural fields can have been removed from the Green Belt while remaining greenfield. Brownfield can also lie within Green Belt. The quarry’s restoration history and the precise development boundary matter. “Brown belt” is not the equivalent planning category.

Do stronger Green Belt affordable rules apply to these schemes?

Current policy GB8 includes affordable provision, infrastructure and accessible green space. Its footnote 43 excludes development on land released through plans adopted before 12 December 2024, and permissions on Green Belt granted before that date. Places for Everyone was adopted in March 2024. It would therefore be misleading to say every listed former Green Belt allocation automatically requires 50% affordable housing. The actual site, date of release, permission and obligations must be checked.

Can infrastructure cope?

The August 2026 infrastructure document is a scoping assessment and coordination framework. It discusses assessment, funding and healthcare planning; it is not proof that every scheme already has funded school places, staffed GP capacity or completed drainage works. The defensible borough-wide conclusion is that support depends on scheme-specific evidence and delivery. This review does not establish that infrastructure either universally supports or universally fails the housing programme.

What evidence would settle the question?

For each scheme, residents need the current decision notice, executed Section 106 agreement, condition-discharge records, affordable tenure schedule and occupation triggers. Infrastructure evidence should cover cumulative traffic, schools including SEND, NHS primary care, drainage and sewer capacity, utilities, public transport, biodiversity and maintenance. A payment or reserved school plot is not the same as an operational service.

Why there is no grand total for these articles

Several entries overlap: Northstone is within South Heywood; Foundry Fields implements the Roch Valley allocation; Barratt’s Stakehill application is within a larger allocation. Lower Falinge replaces existing homes. Completed plots and care-home beds need different treatment. Adding every headline number would produce a misleading total.

Scope and evidence date

Research checked 14 October 2026. This series covers 22 identified major development and regeneration topics across Rochdale borough. It is not a census of every small planning application. Some developments already have occupied homes; asking prices are snapshots. The articles will be updated when outstanding information becomes available.

Secured money, receipts and spending are different

The council’s 2024/25 Infrastructure Funding Statement records £1,522,730 secured through new agreements and £1,629,989 received from agreements across the borough. Of education receipts that year, £619,533 was allocated and none yet spent; separately, £417,976 of older education contributions was spent. It would be false to say no education money was spent. The summary does not identify each development’s payments, school places or occupation triggers. It lists new agreements for Hawks View and Silver Hill, but cannot replace their full signed deeds.

The school forecast is an assessment, not an opening guarantee

The December 2025 primary-school report forecasts Heywood Reception surpluses of 34 in 2026/27, 61 in 2027/28, 29 in 2028/29 and five in 2029/30, with South Heywood housing and school timing to be monitored. For Middleton it forecasts 28 extra places needed in 2026/27, then surpluses of 40, 71 and nine. It discusses additional classes, including use of an existing Hollins classroom; this review does not establish a development-specific approved capital budget or new-school opening from those forecasts. Forecasts are dated planning estimates, not live admissions availability or proof of spare secondary/SEND capacity.

Pennines capacity and the healthcare warning

The school-plan appendix reports, at its assessment date, 75 spare Reception places in North Pennines and 25 in South Pennines, plus 303 spare Key Stage 1 places. Those area figures cannot be treated as guaranteed capacity beside every new estate. For Simister/Bowlee, the NHS’s September 2026 response identifies existing constraints at nearby practices and ongoing assessments, without publishing a funded expansion timetable. Infrastructure support therefore requires more than the existence of nearby schools, surgeries or stations.

Further information and updates

Some final planning agreements, exact rents and prices, affordable-housing breakdowns and infrastructure funding details are not yet available to Rochdale Daily. The relevant articles will be updated when the information becomes available.

articles.title: Rochdale station’s 33 new flats are for private rent: what will tenants actually pay?
articles.excerpt: The Corner Plot scheme near Rochdale station will provide 33 one- and two-bedroom apartments for private rent. Oak Construction Projects is carrying out the build, with Mansell Building Solutions appointed for the specialist frame package.
articles.content_html:
The Corner Plot scheme near Rochdale station will provide 33 one- and two-bedroom apartments for private rent. Oak Construction Projects is carrying out the build, with Mansell Building Solutions appointed for the specialist frame package.

The distinction between private rent and affordable housing matters. A home can cost less than an equivalent Manchester apartment without satisfying the planning definition of affordable housing. No verified monthly rent or service-charge schedule has been established here.

Reporting describes a six-storey development with four commercial units below and net-zero ambitions. Contractor publicity states there are no allocated car-parking spaces and storage for 38 bicycles. The station location supports the transport case, but residents with disabilities, caring commitments or jobs poorly served by public transport need practical arrangements too.

Healthcare capacity and wider neighbourhood services cannot be inferred from railway proximity. The development’s access, tenancy terms, repair responsibilities and actual running costs remain important parts of its offer.

No verified site-specific adverse legal finding against the delivery contractors was established in the sources examined. The construction package should be assessed on its own evidence.

These 33 apartments are separate from Station Gardens’ 81 houses. Both contribute to supply when completed, but neither should be counted twice within broad station-regeneration totals.

Location: Corner of Maclure Road and Station Road, Rochdale

Planning stage: Construction start reported in spring 2026

Homes: 33 apartments, plus commercial space

Let or for sale: Private rent / build to rent; rents and any affordable-rent subset not established

Land: Brownfield redevelopment incorporating refurbishment

Final planning agreement: The executed Section 106 deed, complete schedules, payment triggers and later variations were not verified. This is an evidence gap, not a claim that no agreement exists.

Exact rents / prices: No exact monthly rent, deposit or service-charge schedule is provided in the reviewed announcement/contractor material or established from council/government records.

Affordable breakdown: 33 private-rented flats; no verified planning-defined affordable subset. Private rent must not be relabelled Affordable Rent.

Barratt Redrow joined the CMA’s 2025 commitments settlement, closed without an infringement finding. This does not establish a breach at the local development.

The scheme provides homes in an urban growth area, but remaining completions and restoration progress are the measures needed for an up-to-date assessment.

articles.title: Station Gardens turns former retail land into 81 homes, but the final tenure mix needs to be public
articles.excerpt: Station Gardens is an 81-home development on former Central Retail Park land, delivered through Rochdale Development Agency with Willmott Dixon as contractor. Its announced funding includes £15 million from the Community Regeneration Partnerships Fund, with completion expected in early 2028.
articles.content_html:
Station Gardens is an 81-home development on former Central Retail Park land, delivered through Rochdale Development Agency with Willmott Dixon as contractor. Its announced funding includes £15 million from the Community Regeneration Partnerships Fund, with completion expected in early 2028.

Announcement material describes mixed tenures including social and affordable housing. The public Cabinet record of 23 June 2026 approves housing proposals in principle and delegates final approval; the detailed report is listed as exempt. The final tenure count and household costs therefore cannot be established from that public resolution.

The transport location is one of its principal strengths. Reusing urban land near the station can provide an alternative to greenfield expansion. That advantage still needs accessible routes, adequate services and clarity on any parking restrictions or charges.

Further apartments have appeared in reporting of the wider site. Their capacity and delivery status should be separated from the 81-house construction contract and the 33-apartment Corner Plot project nearby.

No verified site-specific adverse legal finding against the main contractor was established in this review. The funding and environmental claims should be measured against actual completions, energy performance and the costs residents pay.

For the borough’s target, the relevant measure is homes completed in each year. A funded scheme and an announced start provide stronger delivery evidence than an allocation alone, but are not completed housing.

Location: Former Central Retail Park, central Rochdale

Planning stage: Construction start announced November 2025; current progress needs updating

Homes: 81 houses in the delivery phase; further apartment proposals separate

Let or for sale: Mix including social and affordable homes; June 2026 tenure decision needs full verification

Land: Brownfield former retail site

Final planning agreement: The public 23 June 2026 Cabinet minutes record agreement to the housing proposals in principle and delegation of final approval. The detailed tenure/financial report is listed as fully exempt. A later marketing decision for John Rennie Place is scheduled for 27 October 2026, after this article’s evidence date; it is not a completed decision.

Exact rents / prices: Exact rents, sale prices, service charges and plot-by-plot costs are not disclosed in the accessible public Cabinet record reviewed.

Affordable breakdown: Earlier announcements describe mixed tenures including social and affordable homes. The final numerical split cannot be established from the public in-principle resolution or exempt report listing.

Funded school capacity: £15 million Community Regeneration Partnerships funding is announced for the housing project. It is not evidence of a separately funded school expansion; no such scheme-specific capacity commitment verified.

Funded healthcare capacity: No site-specific funded NHS expansion, additional staffed appointment capacity or delivery date was established from the accessible council/government records reviewed. Proximity to a surgery is not a capacity assessment.

Funded transport capacity: Station proximity is an existing accessibility benefit. No new funded service-frequency increase or transport-capacity package established.

articles.title: UK Lawmaker Threatens Visa Bans Over Rochdale Grooming Gang Ringleader
articles.excerpt: A UK lawmaker has warned Pakistan of potential flight and visa bans if it does not accept the return of a ringleader from the Rochdale grooming gang.
articles.content_html:
A UK lawmaker has threatened to impose flight and visa bans on Pakistan if the country does not accept the return of a ringleader from the Rochdale grooming gang. This warning highlights ongoing tensions regarding the handling of individuals involved in serious crimes abroad.

The comments come amid scrutiny of the UK government's approach to dealing with foreign nationals convicted of crimes in the UK. The ringleader, associated with a notorious grooming gang in Rochdale, has reportedly not been returned to Pakistan despite calls for his extradition.

This situation raises concerns about international relations and the management of criminal justice across borders. Local authorities in Rochdale have emphasised the need for effective measures to ensure accountability for those guilty of such crimes, regardless of nationality.

As developments unfold, it remains to be seen how the UK government will respond to Pakistan's stance on this matter.

articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council Publishes Budget Report for 2026/27 to 2028/29
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has published its Budget Report and Medium Term Financial Strategy, outlining financial plans and priorities for the next three years.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has released its Budget Report and Medium Term Financial Strategy for the financial years 2026/27 to 2028/29. This document outlines the council's financial plans and priorities over the next three years.

The report details expected revenue and expenditure, aiming to ensure financial stability and effective service delivery within the borough. It is a crucial step in planning for the future amid ongoing economic challenges.

Local residents and stakeholders are encouraged to review the report, which is available on the council's official website. This transparency allows for community engagement and feedback on the proposed financial strategies.

The council will continue to assess its financial position and make adjustments as necessary, with further updates expected in future council meetings.

Spudbros, a popular jacket potato brand from Preston, has officially opened its new location at the EG Station on Manchester Road in Rochdale. The opening attracted large crowds, with many eager customers queuing for the chance to try the viral spud offerings.

Local residents can now enjoy the convenience of having Spudbros nearby, potentially boosting foot traffic in the area. The new location is likely to become a go-to spot for jacket potato enthusiasts in Rochdale.

articles.title: Rochdale October half-term 2026: school dates and free family activities
articles.excerpt: The council's recommended half-term runs from 26 to 30 October. Here are verified free activities at Rochdale Town Hall, Wardle Library and local family hubs, plus what parents should check before travelling.
articles.content_html:
Families across Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough and Milnrow can start planning the October school break, with the council recommending Monday 26 to Friday 30 October 2026 as the autumn half-term holiday. The dates are a borough-wide recommended pattern, rather than a guarantee for every school, so parents should check their own school's calendar before booking childcare or a trip.

One of the clearest free options announced so far is at Rochdale Town Hall. Its Spooktacular Half Term programme is advertised for every day from Monday 26 October to Sunday 1 November, running from 10am to 4pm at the Town Hall on The Esplanade, OL16 1AZ. The organiser describes family-friendly Halloween activities, with free entry and no advance booking required. More detailed individual activities have not yet all been listed, so it is worth checking the official Town Hall event information before travelling.

For families wanting a short outing at the end of the break, Wardle Library's Kids' Club is listed in the council's October events calendar for Saturday 31 October. The free session runs from 10am until 12.30pm at 448 Birch Road, Wardle, OL12 9LH. It is aimed at families with children aged four and over and normally includes crafts, activities and challenges. The council says there is no need to book.

Parents and carers with younger children also have the borough's family hubs to investigate. Council information lists activities for children aged up to five at locations including Heybrook, Howard Street, Meanwood, Castleton, Deeplish and Sandbrook, as well as centres in Middleton, Heywood, Littleborough and the wider Pennines area. The council describes these activities as free unless otherwise stated. The listing is a directory rather than a confirmed half-term timetable, so families should consult their nearest hub's current programme instead of assuming ordinary weekly sessions continue during the holiday.

Not every regular children's library session runs during school holidays. Some Bookstart activities are explicitly described as term-time sessions, making it especially important to check dates rather than turn up on the strength of a weekly listing.

Parents trying to keep costs down can therefore rely on the confirmed free Town Hall programme and check the Wardle Library listing, while using the council's event directory to see whether anything else is added nearer the time. This guide covers confirmed information available on 13 October; opening arrangements and individual sessions may change.

Useful official sources: Rochdale Borough Council's 2026–27 school holiday calendar; the council's Spooktacular Half Term at Rochdale Town Hall listing; the council's libraries events calendar and Wardle Kids' Club entry; and the council's Family Hub Activities directory. Verify any last-minute change with the organiser before setting off.

articles.title: Rochdale to Host Ignite Fire Festival Ahead of Christmas Lights Switch-On
articles.excerpt: The Ignite Fire Festival will return to Rochdale from November 20 to 22, featuring a new immersive trail and a Fire Garden, promising a spectacular start to the festive season.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale is set to kick off its Christmas festivities with the Ignite Fire Festival, taking place from Friday, November 20, to Sunday, November 22. The event will transform the square and gardens around Rochdale Town Hall into a magical experience filled with fire, lights, and sound, running each evening from 5pm to 8pm.

Organised by the Rochdale Development Agency, this year's festival promises to be the best yet, featuring new attractions including an immersive night-time trail called ‘BODY’. This installation will guide visitors through six zones of the human body using fire, light, sound, and special effects, marking its north-west premiere after successful runs in locations from Ireland to Canada.

In addition to the trail, attendees can explore a Fire Garden, which will illuminate the slopes and gardens behind Rochdale Town Hall with intricate hand-crafted fire sculptures and pyrotechnics, creating a captivating visual display.

The Ignite Fire Festival is a free event, and organisers encourage residents and visitors alike to come and enjoy the festive atmosphere as the town prepares for the Christmas season.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Town gets ready to ignite Christmas festivities - Rochdale Times Skip to content LATEST NEWS , OUT AND ABOUT Town gets ready to ignite Christmas festivities The countdown to Christmas begins in spectacular style next month with the return of the Ignite Fire Festival leading up to the festive lights switch-on. Ignite Fire Festival will again be transforming the square and gardens around Rochdale Town Hall, including the new pathways and parkland on Broadfield Slopes. This free night-time event will open over three evenings from Friday, November 20, to Sunday, November 22, from 5pm to 8pm, delivering a magical trail of fire, lights and sound. Organisers Rochdale Development Agency are promising this year will be the best yet with new dazzling trails and attractions. New for this year, the immersive night-time trail ‘BODY’ will take centre stage. It will bring visitors on a journey through six zones of the human body using fire, light, sound and special effects. Organisers Rochdale Development Agency are promising this year will be the best yet. (Photograph courtesy of Naoise Culhane) The multi-sensory experience is the most ambitious fire and light installation yet from multi-award-winning outdoor arts specialists Walk the Plank, and Ignite will be its north-west premiere, after having previously travelled over the globe, from Ireland to Canada. There will also be a Fire Garden providing extra sparkle, illuminating slopes and gardens behind Rochdale Town Hall with intricate hand-crafted fire sculptures and pyrotechnics, transforming it into a place of beauty. Back again for 2026 is Drum Machine — the 20-strong drumming collective who will be bringing their dance floor grooves and stomping tunes to the event. READ MORE: Residents warned over repairs claims firm Also returning are Fireflies as part of the Culture Co-op programme with Rochdale’s Skylight Circus Arts and live fire shows by interactive arts group Travelling Light Circus, alongside residents trained up especially for the festival performing mesmerising fire spinning feats. There will also be flame-cooked hot food served each night, mulled wine and other seasonal drinks. The free night-time event will open over 3 evenings from Friday, 20 to Sunday, 22 November 2026. (Photograph courtesy of Neil McElmon) On Sunday, November 22, Father Christmas and his special guests, including the Mayor of Rochdale Councillor Faisal Rana, will officially switch-on the lights at 5.30pm in front of the town hall after the traditional countdown, whilst Ignite Fire Festival continues until 8pm. Cllr Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation at Rochdale Council said: “Ignite Fire Festival has become a real success story for the borough, drawing audiences from across Greater Manchester and beyond. “This 2026 line-up will build on that success with new attractions, creative performances and family-friendly experiences. It will be a fantastic celebration for residents and visitors alike, setting the stage perfectly for our Christmas lights switch-on.” Bev Ayre, senior producer at Walk the Plank, said the group is delighted to be returning to Rochdale. “The Body is unlike anything we’ve brought to Ignite before. An immersive fire and light experience that combines art, science and creativity to help people discover the incredible human body in a fun and engaging way. Set against the stunning backdrop of Rochdale Town Hall Square and gardens, it promises to be one of our most exciting attractions yet. Even if you’ve visited Ignite before, this year’s festival will feel completely new.” Ignite Fire Festival is now one of the borough’s most popular free events. articles.title: Canine Country Club in Rochdale Launches New Classes After Passing Licence Inspection
articles.excerpt: Canine Country Club has introduced new puppy sessions and enrichment classes following a successful animal activities licence inspection, enhancing its services for local dog owners.
articles.content_html:
Canine Country Club, located in Rochdale, has announced the launch of new puppy sessions and individual enrichment classes after successfully passing its first animal activities licence inspection. The owner, Stefanie, who recently took over the business, expressed her excitement in a message to customers, stating, "I am thrilled to share that we passed!"

The new puppy programmes will be held on Thursdays from 10am to noon, providing a structured environment for young dogs to learn and socialise. In addition to these sessions, the club will offer one-to-one enrichment classes designed for dogs that may be timid, less social, or older, allowing them to engage in activities in a quieter setting.

Stefanie emphasised that the welfare of the dogs is her top priority, stating, "Providing a welfare-focused program that prioritises the dogs' best interests has always been my top priority." This initiative aims to cater to the diverse needs of dogs in the community, ensuring they receive the attention and care they require.

Local dog owners interested in these new classes can contact Canine Country Club for further information and to book their spots. The introduction of these classes is expected to enhance the services available to pet owners in Rochdale, providing valuable opportunities for socialisation and enrichment for their dogs.

articles.title: Delays on Rochdale East Didsbury Line Due to Track Obstruction
articles.excerpt: Tram services on the Rochdale East Didsbury line are delayed following an obstruction on the tracks, with further disruptions across the network due to a road traffic collision.
articles.content_html:
Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) has reported delays on the Rochdale East Didsbury tram line due to an object blocking the tracks. The disruption was noted on Tuesday, 13 October, at approximately 4:56pm and is expected to continue until further notice.

In addition to the delays on the Rochdale line, no trams are currently operating on the Eccles, Trafford Centre, and Altrincham lines. Passengers may need to use alternative transport options, including express shuttle buses, trains, or Bee Network buses to complete their journeys.

Furthermore, there are ongoing delays on the Eccles line due to a previous road traffic collision, with tickets and passes valid on several bus routes, including the 10, 30, 33, 50, 52, 53, 67, 79, 100, 248, and 249 services.

Passengers are advised to plan their journeys ahead of time and can contact the Metrolink customer service for assistance, especially as the lift at Besses o' th' Barn tram stop is out of service. The contact number for the Metrolink is 0161 244 1000, available from 7am to 8pm on weekdays and 8am to 8pm on weekends and bank holidays.

articles.title: Rossendale RUFC Defeats Rochdale in Local Derby
articles.excerpt: Rossendale RUFC secured a victory over Rochdale in a closely contested local derby, overcoming an early setback to win the match last weekend.
articles.content_html:
Rossendale RUFC returned to winning form with a hard-fought victory against Rochdale in a local derby held last weekend. The match, which saw both teams displaying strong performances, began with Rochdale taking an early lead, scoring straight from the kick-off.

The Stags quickly responded, equalising through Junior Nuu, who capitalised on a gap in the Rochdale defence to score a try, followed by a successful conversion from Will Hunt, bringing the score to 7-7. However, Rochdale regained the lead shortly after, scoring again to make it 14-7.

As the match progressed, Rossendale began to apply consistent pressure on Rochdale's defence. This effort paid off when winger Terence Babarinsa scored a second try for Rossendale, narrowing the gap and shifting the momentum in their favour.

The victory is significant for Rossendale RUFC as they aim to improve their standing in the league. The next fixture for Rossendale will be crucial as they look to build on this success and continue their push for a stronger season.

articles.title: Breaking news: Rochdale Daily reaches 86,000 readers in 30 days — thank you, Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Daily is celebrating 86,000 readers in the last 30 days, thanking the borough for its support and setting an ambitious goal of reaching 200,000 readers by November.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Daily has reached an incredible milestone: 86,000 readers over the past 30 days. To every person who has opened one of our articles, shared a story, sent us an email or helped us reach a neighbour — thank you.

We are humbled. We are grateful. And, most of all, we are delighted that so many people across our borough have chosen to make Rochdale Daily part of their day.

We built this independent newspaper around a simple belief: Rochdale deserves local news that is open, accessible and free from party-political allegiance. We want to bring you unfiltered reporting — stories that celebrate our communities, champion our businesses, ask difficult questions and hold public institutions to account without telling readers what they should think.

Eighty-six thousand readers in a month means something to us because behind every number is a person: a parent checking what is happening at school, a resident following a council decision, a family looking for something to do, a small business hoping to be noticed or a neighbour who simply wants to understand the place they call home.

We want you to know that we read every email. We value your tips, your corrections, your concerns and your encouragement. Some of the stories that matter most begin when one resident takes the time to get in touch.

And we have a big ambition for what comes next: to reach 200,000 readers by November. It is an ambitious target, not a forecast, but we want more people across Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough, Milnrow and the wider borough to know that their local stories have a home here.

If you have enjoyed an article, please leave a comment. If you disagree, tell us why. If something important is happening in your street or community, get in touch. Follow the Rochdale Daily Facebook page and share our articles with friends, family and neighbours.

Your comments, questions and suggestions help shape what we investigate and where we direct our attention. We won't always get everything right, and when we don't, we want to hear about it, correct mistakes and do better.

We do not want this to be a newspaper that talks at Rochdale. We want it to be a newspaper that listens to Rochdale.

To all 86,000 of you: thank you for putting your trust in us. We intend to work to earn it every day.

Please comment, follow, share and stay with us. This is your newspaper. We want to work for you — and for our town.

With heartfelt thanks, the Rochdale Daily team.

Read more at rochdaledaily.co.uk. Send stories, corrections and feedback to news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.
