articles.title: BREAKING INVESTIGATION: £50.3m owed by Rochdale Council companies as £19.5m Council Tax shortfall raises scrutiny
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's draft accounts show £50.309m in Upperbanks company loan balances, £2.02m interest added and only £132,000 repaid in 2025/26. We examine the figures, the 2022 decisions and the councillors responsible for oversight.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING INVESTIGATION | ROCHDALE DAILY

Rochdale Borough Council's own draft accounts reveal that three companies behind the Upperbanks development owed it £50.309 million in contractual loans at 31 March 2026. In the preceding financial year, just £132,000 was repaid while £2.020 million in interest accrued, increasing the total balance from £48.262 million.

The figures sit alongside reporting that the borough accumulated a £19.5 million Council Tax collection shortfall over the decade since 2016. These are very different forms of money: Council Tax is revenue for services, while Upperbanks loans finance long-term property assets and are not necessarily due for repayment now. Yet both invite scrutiny of how the authority manages public finances.

Source: Rochdale Borough Council, draft Statement of Accounts 2025/26, note on soft loans, printed page 81: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/downloads/file/3217/2025-2026-statement-of-accounts-draft-

Source: Roch Valley Radio, 'Council tax shortfall in Rochdale of almost £20m in 10 years', 12 June 2026: https://www.rochvalleyradio.com/news/local-news/council-tax-shortfall-in-rochdale-of-almost-20m-in-10-years/

WHAT IS UPPERBANKS AND HOW MUCH IS OWED?

The £60 million Upperbanks scheme, beside Rochdale Riverside, comprises 242 rental apartments and a 146-room Hampton by Hilton hotel. The development received more than £17 million from the Future High Streets Fund and over £3 million from Greater Manchester's Brownfield Development Fund. The hotel opened in September 2023.

The council's soft-loan table shows £33.662 million owed by Rochdale BTR Ltd on a property loan and £2.045 million in its working-capital borrowing. Rochdale Hotel Holdings Ltd had a £14.270 million property loan and Rochdale Hotel Ltd owed £332,000 in working capital. Together, these total £50.309 million.

The original loan arrangements included payment-holiday periods under which interest accrued and was added to the loans. The council also confirms the lending was provided below market rates in support of its service priorities. That means a growing balance is not, by itself, proof that any company has missed a scheduled payment. The critical missing information is the agreed repayment profile and actual cash returned to the council.

Source: Council draft accounts, printed page 81: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/downloads/file/3217/2025-2026-statement-of-accounts-draft-

Source: Rochdale Development Agency, Upperbanks project details: https://investinrochdale.co.uk/regeneration/projects/upperbanks

THE £2 MILLION INTEREST QUESTION

The 2025/26 loan schedule lists £2.020 million of accrued interest, £159,000 in new advances and £132,000 in repayments. Net contractual loans increased by £2.047 million. The £2.020 million interest recorded is more than fifteen times that year's total repayments.

However, the same page contains an apparent inconsistency. Its narrative says 'no new advances were made', while the adjoining table shows £159,000 of advances to Rochdale BTR Ltd's working-capital loan. The council should reconcile the entries and specify whether the amount was new cash, a transfer or an accounting classification.

The accounts also put the soft loans at a far lower carrying amount, £22.690 million, because below-market loans are discounted for accounting purposes. The council says the concessionary benefit to its subsidiaries is treated as an additional investment; the value of that investment is stated as £27.3 million. The difference is not a £27 million write-off: it reflects accounting treatment of long-term, below-market lending.

WHAT ABOUT THE RISK OF NON-REPAYMENT?

The council's draft accounts record a £472,000 expected-credit-loss allowance across relevant loans at 31 March 2026, of which £267,000 relates to the hotel companies, £189,000 to Rochdale BTR Ltd and £16,000 to other loans. The allowance increased by a net £37,000 during 2025/26. This is a forward-looking credit-risk provision, not proof that a borrower has defaulted or that £472,000 has been lost.

Source: Council draft accounts, printed page 89, impairment table: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/downloads/file/3217/2025-2026-statement-of-accounts-draft-

ARE THE APARTMENTS AND HOTEL DELIVERING?

According to Rochdale Development Agency's fourth-quarter delivery plan, 155 of the 242 Upperbanks apartments were occupied on 24 March 2026, with eight more reserved. That left 87 unoccupied at the reporting date, although occupancy had improved from earlier in the year. The agency also reported improving hotel occupancy, average room rates and yields. The public report did not supply a complete profit-and-loss or cash-flow analysis establishing whether the companies were meeting their initial business cases.

Source: Rochdale Development Agency 2025/26 Q4 delivery plan: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s122466/2025-26%20RDA%20Delivery%20Plan%20Q4%20FINAL.pdf

WHICH COUNCILLORS WERE INVOLVED — AND WHICH PARTIES?

The scheme's corporate and funding decisions were considered under a Labour-controlled Rochdale Council led by Councillor Neil Emmott (Labour). Councillor John Blundell (Labour and Co-operative) held the Economy and Regeneration portfolio in 2022, when the Upperbanks proposals came before Cabinet. Councillor Carol Wardle (Labour) held the Finance and Corporate portfolio then and continues as the Finance and Growth portfolio holder in 2026.

Councillor Daniel Meredith (Labour and Co-operative), now the Cabinet Member for Regeneration and Housing, has a different documented voting history: minutes of the 22 November 2022 Cabinet meeting state that he expressly requested his vote AGAINST the Upperbanks loan agreement be recorded. The minutes do not specify why he objected, and he must not be portrayed as having approved that agreement.

The 2022 decision approved a loan agreement while delegating the detail of its terms and structure to officers in consultation with relevant portfolio holders. The politicians' portfolios identify responsibility for decisions and oversight, but do not individually establish blame for any loss or wrongdoing.

Source: Rochdale Council, Cabinet meeting of 22 November 2022, item 19: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieIssueDetails.aspx?IId=51234&Opt=3&PlanId=0

Source: Rochdale Council, May 2026 Cabinet appointments: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieListDocuments.aspx?CId=156&MeetingId=7146

Source: Rochdale Council, Cabinet portfolio responsibilities: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/mgCommitteeDetails.aspx?ID=116

WHY ARE FINANCIAL FORECASTS RESTRICTED?

On 5 February 2026, Cabinet received an Upperbanks trading-company financial update including forecasts compared with the business cases approved in June 2022. The published decision notes that the council is the ultimate parent undertaking and 100% shareholder. But detailed financial enclosures were restricted from public view, leaving the public unable to independently compare the original profitability, occupancy and repayment forecasts with current performance.

Source: Cabinet decision, 5 February 2026: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieDecisionDetails.aspx?AIId=49322

THE COUNCIL TAX COMPARISON — WHAT IT DOES AND DOES NOT SHOW

Roch Valley Radio reported that the £19.5 million figure was a cumulative Council Tax collection shortfall since 2016, drawn from 2024/25 accounts, including about £1.3 million in 2024/25. It is not evidence of a fresh £19.5 million hole in the council's 2026/27 budget, and should not be directly subtracted from or compared with Upperbanks' contractual loan book as though both were immediately available cash.

The comparison does raise a narrower, evidence-based question: how transparent is the council about its own long-term financial commitments, loan repayments and commercial outcomes while it seeks to maximise Council Tax collection?

QUESTIONS REQUIRING ANSWERS

Rochdale Daily is seeking clarity on the contractual repayment timetable, how much loan interest has actually been received in cash, the latest independent valuations of Upperbanks' assets, the trading companies' current profitability, the £159,000 'new advances' discrepancy, and whether a non-confidential comparison with the original 2022 business cases will be released.

Councillor Meredith's recorded vote against the original loan agreement also merits an explanation of his reasons at the time, without assuming those reasons.

Upperbanks has delivered homes and a hotel to the town centre, while published occupancy data show improvement. Neither physical regeneration nor a large outstanding loan balance alone establishes that the scheme has succeeded or failed financially. The public accounts do, however, make a compelling case for clear reporting of when public funds are expected to be repaid and whether the original forecasts are being met.

This investigation is based on the council's DRAFT 2025/26 accounts, which remain subject to audit. Neither the loan balances nor the credit-loss allowances establish unlawful conduct, fraud or improper spending.

Right of reply: Rochdale Borough Council, the named councillors and the Upperbanks companies can send a response, correction or supporting financial evidence to news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

articles.title: Bus Services Suspended Between Rochdale Town Centre and Freehold Following Collision
articles.excerpt: A road traffic collision at Westwood has led to the suspension of bus services between Rochdale Town Centre and Freehold, with ticket acceptance in place on multiple routes.
articles.content_html:
A road traffic collision at Westwood has resulted in the suspension of bus services between Rochdale Town Centre and Freehold. The incident has disrupted travel for many commuters.

In response to the disruption, Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) has implemented ticket acceptance on several bus services. Affected routes include the 17, 57, 59, 76, 76A, 81, 83, 84, 114, 149, 181, 182, 409, 411, 435, 436, and 471.

Passengers are advised to check the TfGM travel alerts page for updates on the situation and any changes to service availability. The collision has caused significant delays, and it is currently unclear when normal service will resume.

Local residents and commuters may experience longer journey times due to the disruption. TfGM is working to resolve the situation as quickly as possible.

articles.title: Rochdale Pioneers Museum Hosts Archive Sessions on Local Folklore
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale Pioneers Museum will hold free drop-in sessions this weekend, exploring traditional and supernatural tales from the borough's archives, led by Mitch Robinson.
articles.content_html:
The Rochdale Pioneers Museum will host free archive creative drop-in sessions this weekend, focusing on traditional, unusual, and even supernatural tales from the borough's archives. The sessions, led by Mitch Robinson, aim to uncover hidden stories and records, ranging from folklore to magical narratives.

Scheduled for Saturday, October 15, the hour-long sessions will take place at 12.30pm and 2pm, with no prior booking required. Participants will have the opportunity to engage with old books, documents, and letters that often remain stored away, providing a unique insight into the area's history.

The Co-op Heritage Trust, which is facilitating the event, encourages anyone interested in storytelling, history, or creativity to attend. The sessions are particularly suitable for families with older children, as they will delve into themes of folk belief, magic, and the supernatural.

This initiative is part of the 'Open with Care!' programme, designed to inspire and engage the community during the spooky season. Attendees can expect a creative and thought-provoking experience, whether they are history enthusiasts or simply looking for an intriguing activity this weekend.

articles.title: Rochdale AFC Women Exit FA Cup After Defeat to Atherton
articles.excerpt: Rochdale AFC Women were eliminated from the Women's FA Cup following a defeat against Atherton on Sunday, October 12.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale AFC Women faced a disappointing exit from the Women's FA Cup after losing to Atherton on Sunday, October 12. The match took place at Atherton's home ground, where the Dale women struggled against a determined opposition.

Despite a strong start, Rochdale were unable to convert their chances into goals, ultimately succumbing to Atherton's effective counter-attacks. The final score reflected the hosts' dominance, leaving Rochdale to reflect on missed opportunities.

This defeat marks the end of Rochdale's FA Cup journey for this season, with the team now focusing on their league commitments. Fans will be keen to see how the team responds in their next match as they aim to regroup and build momentum.

articles.title: Why Rochdale says “cruckle”
articles.excerpt: How a tiny local verb — to “cruckle” — links everyday speech in Rochdale to older northern dialects and why linguists care.
articles.summary: How a tiny local verb — to “cruckle” — links everyday speech in Rochdale to older northern dialects and why linguists care.
articles.body:
Anyone from Rochdale who’s ever limped away from a small mishap will recognise the line: “I cruckled my ankle.” For many locals, cruckle means the particular half‑twist or awkward roll of the foot you can often walk off — not a full sprain but a sudden wobble that makes you wince. This usage is recorded in contemporary perceptual descriptions of Greater Manchester speech and has been listed by residents when describing Rochdale’s spoken character. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

The word itself, however, has deeper roots. Historical dialect lexicography gives us a family of related forms — crookle, crukle, cruggle, krukel — all clustered around meanings such as to bend, make crooked, stoop, huddle or hobble. Late‑19th and early‑20th‑century dialect sources and Scottish dialect records preserve these cognates, showing the same phonetic shape and similar senses across northern English and Scots varieties. In the Dictionary of the Scots Language you can see cognate entries (kruggle / cruggle / cruckle) used with senses like “to crouch or huddle,” and nineteenth‑century dialect glosses list crookle with senses such as “to make crooked; to bend, twist.” ([dsl.ac.uk](https://dsl.ac.uk/entry/snd00075099))

How did a general sense of bending or crookedness come to mean the small ankle‑roll in Rochdale? Linguists point to ordinary, well‑attested word‑formation processes. A crook/crook‑ family root (suggesting bending, hooking or crookedness) plus a frequentative or diminutive ‑le ending can produce verbs that describe small, repeated, or imitative actions — crook → crookle. Comparable northern and Germanic dialect forms show similar semantic shifts from ‘bend’ or ‘stoop’ toward senses connected with awkward gait or limping; the broader comparative work on Germanic dialect vocabularies helps explain why these forms and meanings sit together. In short, cruckle is linguistically predictable as a local survival and narrowing of an older dialect verb family. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/be/The_semantic_development_of_words_for_%22walk%2C_run%22_in_the_Germanic_languages_%28IA_semanticdevelopm00ihririch%29.pdf))

Is cruckle uniquely Rochdalian? The short answer is: socially, yes — geographically, not absolutely. Perceptual dialect research carried out in Greater Manchester (2024) collected people’s mental maps and comments about local speech; among the keywords used to evoke Rochdale speech were “broad,” “flat,” “guinnel” and “cruckle,” showing that residents and neighbours associate the word particularly with Rochdale. That kind of folk‑linguistic visibility gives a strong local identity to a word even when related forms appear in older records elsewhere. At the same time, historical dictionaries and place‑name evidence show related spellings and senses across northern England and Scotland, so it would be misleading to claim the sound‑type has never occurred outside the area. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

Large projects that collect lived speech and crowd‑sourced dialect entries also help explain how such words persist. When the British Library and other public call‑outs gathered regional words, contributors highlighted locally specific items that researchers had not always recorded in older printed dialect dictionaries; popular reportage of that work singled out “cruckle” as an example of a recognisably local term with onomatopoeic appeal. These crowdsourced attestations, together with formal perceptual surveys, are why small words like cruckle keep turning up in contemporary studies of regional identity. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/nov/24/british-library-project-discovers-two-new-words-thanks-to-guardian-readers))

What should readers take away? Cruckle matters because it shows how vocabulary anchors place: the word’s form and original sense are old and shared across northern dialects, but memory, everyday use and local attitude have made it feel distinctly Rochdale. Linguists view it as a useful data point — for historical contact between Lancashire and Yorkshire varieties, for small‑scale semantic narrowing, and for how people use language to say where they’re from. If you’ve got family pronunciations, old spellings or written examples from letters, keep them — local archives and dialect projects welcome material that helps trace exactly when and where words like cruckle shifted meaning and stuck to a place.

articles.title: Rochdale Council to Implement New Planning Decision Rules from October 31
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council will shift more planning applications to officers under new rules effective from October 31, aiming to streamline decision-making and focus committees on larger proposals.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council is set to implement revised planning decision procedures starting October 31, 2026. The new rules will see a significant shift in how planning applications are processed, with more decisions being made by planning officers rather than elected committees. This change follows the Government's guidance under the Town and Country Planning (Discharge of Local Planning Authority Functions) (England) Regulations 2026.

Under the new system, applications will be categorised into two schedules. Schedule One will include householder applications, minor commercial and residential proposals, lawful development certificates, and technical matters, all of which must be determined by planning officers. Schedule Two will encompass larger developments, listed building consents, advertisement consents, tree preservation orders, and legal agreements with developers, which can be referred to the planning committee but require agreement between a nominated councillor and a nominated officer.

The council's report indicates that the Government aims to provide greater clarity regarding the role of planning committees, allowing them to focus on significant proposals while routine decisions are handled by officers. Councillors will still be able to engage with planning matters, raise residents' concerns, and submit material planning reasons, but a councillor's request alone will not necessitate committee consideration. Additionally, the previous threshold for the number of objections required to trigger committee review will no longer apply.

The council has warned that decisions made by planning committees on applications that should be handled by officers could face legal challenges, potentially leading to judicial reviews. As the new rules come into effect, residents and stakeholders in Rochdale will need to be aware of these changes and their implications for local planning processes.

articles.title: Rochdale research centre moves closer to opening with £107m economic ambition
articles.excerpt: The Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre at Kingsway Business Park has completed its main building, with specialist fit-out ahead of a planned 2027 opening.
articles.content_html:
A new Rochdale facility designed to help turn scientific discoveries into commercial products has reached a construction milestone, ahead of a planned opening in 2027.

The main building of the Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre, at Kingsway Business Park, is now complete. Specialist equipment and facilities will be installed before it becomes operational.

The centre will support work on advanced materials with potential applications in medicine, electronics and construction, helping researchers test whether ideas developed in laboratories can become practical products.

Scientists and businesses will work with the University of Manchester and specialist innovation partners, connecting research expertise with the facilities needed to develop and manufacture new technologies.

The 30,000 sq ft centre is the first major physical development within the Atom Valley Innovation District, bringing researchers, manufacturers and investors together in Rochdale.

Independent analysis cited by the project’s partners forecasts £107 million in economic value over ten years, alongside opportunities to attract investment, businesses and skilled employment. That figure is a forecast, rather than income already generated.

Professor John Holden, the University of Manchester’s vice-president for civic engagement and innovation, said the next challenge was to connect the building with businesses, research and expertise to create lasting benefits.

For Rochdale, the centre represents a step towards establishing a larger advanced manufacturing sector—although its laboratories are still being prepared for the work ahead.

articles.title: ‘Really nice’: an editor’s visit to the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Daily's editor visited the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road with her little girl and found kind, efficient staff, a fully available menu and a welcome that earned a child's verdict: ‘really nice’.
articles.content_html:
There are plenty of ways to judge a new coffee shop. You can look at the menu, the speed of the service or whether it manages to make a quick stop feel pleasant. But after visiting the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road with my little girl, I found that the most telling review came from her.

“Really nice,” she said of the people working there. Two words, and a rather lovely assessment.

As the editor of Rochdale Daily, I spend a great deal of time looking at what opens, closes and changes across the borough. This time, rather than reporting on a launch, I wanted to experience the place as an ordinary customer — and a parent.

What stood out was the staff. They were kind, welcoming and efficient, handling our visit with the sort of ease that makes all the difference when you have a child alongside you. Good service does not need to be theatrical. Often, it is simply being treated warmly while everything runs as it should.

The full menu was available during our visit, too. There were no disappointing discoveries that something we wanted could not be ordered. It is a simple thing, but it matters: choice is only useful when the items are actually available.

The branch, which opened in August near Rochdale Infirmary and Dunelm, provides both indoor seating and a drive-through. For people visiting the hospital, passing along Whitworth Road or simply looking for a coffee stop, those options are convenient. But convenience alone is not what makes a customer want to return.

Children have an uncomplicated way of measuring an experience. They remember whether somebody was kind. They notice when they are made to feel welcome. My little girl did not care about the branding or the opening ceremony; she cared that the people were, in her words, “really nice”.

This was one family visit, not a claim that every visit will be identical. But the team deserve credit for getting the fundamentals right: kindness, efficiency and a menu we could actually order from.

Sometimes a new business makes its best first impression not through a grand announcement but through the people behind the counter. On our visit to Whitworth Road, Starbucks did exactly that.

Editor’s note: This is a first-hand editorial account of a visit, not a paid advertisement. For the original opening report, see Rochdale Daily’s article, “New Starbucks Drive-Through Opens on Whitworth Road”.

articles.title: Rochdale Council to Consider Motion to Reassess Climate Targets Amid Cost-of-Living Crisis
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council will discuss a motion from Cllr John Taylor on 13 October, urging a shift in focus from climate targets to addressing the cost-of-living crisis affecting residents.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council is set to discuss a motion on 13 October that calls for a reassessment of its climate emergency targets in light of the ongoing cost-of-living crisis. The motion, proposed by Councillor John Taylor, suggests that the council prioritise immediate support for residents over its commitment to environmental goals.

In 2019, the council declared a climate emergency and pledged to achieve carbon neutrality by 2038. However, Cllr Taylor argues that the local impact on carbon reduction has been minimal and that resources could be better allocated to address pressing economic challenges faced by the community.

The council meeting will also include updates on initiatives such as the expansion of the electric vehicle charging network and the Rochdale Town Centre Heat Network, which aims to utilise heat from sewers to reduce energy costs for buildings. The council has received a £1 million grant from the Government to support this project and will soon begin seeking a development partner.

As the council considers this motion, residents may be interested in how these discussions could influence future policies and support measures during the current economic climate.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Council called on to ‘scrap climate targets and focus on cost-of-living crisis’ - Rochdale Times Skip to content LATEST NEWS Council called on to ‘scrap climate targets and focus on cost-of-living crisis’ Rochdale Council is being called on to put helping residents during the cost-of-living crisis ahead of meeting environmental targets. When Rochdale’s full council meets on Thursday, it will consider a motion from Cllr John Taylor calling on the authority to rescind its commitment to climate emergency targets. The meeting will also hear updates on expanding the electric vehicle charging network and the Rochdale Town Centre Heat Network which will see heat from sewers beneath Rochdale will be harnessed to cut energy costs and keep buildings warm. The council has received a £1 million commercialisation grant from Government and will begin a tender for a development partner to take the scheme forward and prepare it for construction. Cllr Taylor’s motion reads: “In 2019 this council, in line with national trends, passed a climate emergency motion and committed resources (financial and human) to achieving carbon neutrality. “A key element of the motion was the inclusion of a Carbon Neutral Target which pledged to make both the council’s operations and the wider borough carbon neutral by 2038. “Since 2019 it has become clear that our local impact on carbon reduction is negligible and it does not represent the most efficient use of our resources. READ MORE: Heat from sewers will keep Rochdale warm in future “Consequently, it is appropriate to review our commitment to carbon neutrality and dispense with our 2019 pledge. “This council recognises the direct impact that the cost-of-living crisis and housing emergency have on many residents, and they must be our strategic priorities alongside the efficient and effective delivery of our core services. Future efforts to achieve carbon neutrality must also be cost neutral. “A local repeal will not override national legislation; the UK remains legally bound by the Climate Change Act to reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. “This is not a withdrawal from environmental action nor a belief that climate change is not a serious issue. It is a recognition of what is within our capacity to change and a renewed focus on deploying our controllable resources.” By rescinding the commitment to all climate emergency targets, Cllr Taylor hopes the council will direct resources to address the cost-of-living crisis and housing emergency. By reviewing all ongoing climate, carbon-neutrality activity, Cllr Taylor wants to stop any programmes that cannot demonstrate a “clear resident benefit, financial saving or statutory requirement”. articles.title: Rochdale Draw 1-1 with Tranmere to Extend Unbeaten Run in League Two
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's unbeaten streak in League Two continues as they secure a 1-1 draw against Tranmere at Prenton Park, with Dajaune Brown equalising after Tom Conlon's opening goal.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale extended their unbeaten League Two run to five games with a 1-1 draw against Tranmere Rovers at Prenton Park on Saturday. The match saw Tom Conlon give the hosts an early lead before Dajaune Brown equalised in the second half, ensuring Dale maintained their impressive form.

Conlon opened the scoring for Tranmere in the 15th minute, capitalising on a defensive error by Rochdale. After the visitors allowed the ball to go out for a throw-in, Conlon struck from 25 yards, finding the top-left corner of the net. Tranmere could have increased their lead before half-time, but Tom Ince missed a close-range opportunity, and Dylan Jones fired wide under pressure from Aden Flint just before the break.

The second half saw Rochdale respond positively, with Brown scoring the equaliser in the 57th minute. He tapped home from close range after connecting with a cross from Charlie Tasker. Tranmere continued to press for a second goal, with Ince's long-range effort hitting the underside of the bar, but Rochdale held firm to secure a point.

This draw leaves Tranmere winless in their last five matches, having recorded six draws this season. Rochdale's next fixture will be crucial as they look to build on their current form and continue their push up the League Two table.

articles.excerpt: Police are seeking help from the public to locate Sean, a 22-year-old man who went missing in Rochdale's Milkstone area on October 20. Family members describe his disappearance as unusual and urge anyone with information to come forward.
articles.content_html:

Police are seeking help from the public to locate Sean, a 22-year-old man who went missing in Rochdale's Milkstone area on October 20. Family members describe his disappearance as unusual and urge anyone with information to come forward.

Greater Manchester Police have issued an urgent appeal for help in locating Kody, a 16-year-old girl missing since Friday morning in the Norden area of Rochdale.

Police in Rochdale have launched an urgent appeal for information regarding the whereabouts of a 22-year-old man named Sean, who has gone missing. He was last seen in the Milkstone area of Rochdale town centre at approximately 7am on October 20, 2026.

Sean is described as white, with a slim build, standing around 5ft 9in tall. He has dark hair and a thick moustache. At the time of his disappearance, he was wearing a distinctive black Moncler jacket made from shiny material, a black bodywarmer, and black trousers.

Family members have expressed their concern, stating that Sean's disappearance is unusual for him. They are pleading with the public to share the appeal widely in hopes of locating him quickly. They have not provided a last name for Sean, but they are urging anyone who may have seen him or has information about his whereabouts to come forward.

Anyone with information about Sean's whereabouts is urged to contact Greater Manchester Police by calling 0161 856 8643 and quoting log number 110-211026. The police are keen to hear from anyone who may have seen him or has any information that could assist in locating him.

articles.title: New Support Website Launched for Survivors of Child Sexual Abuse in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: A new website, IAmReady.org, offers tailored support for survivors of child sexual abuse and exploitation, providing resources to help them navigate investigations and review closed cases.
articles.content_html:
Survivors of child sexual abuse and exploitation in Rochdale can now access a new support service designed to help them understand their options regarding investigations into their allegations. The website, IAmReady.org, offers tailored advice and guidance based on individual needs, enabling victims to make informed decisions about their cases.

Developed in collaboration with survivors, the website provides trauma-informed information in an accessible format. Users can navigate the site at their own pace, with features that allow them to save their progress and exit quickly for privacy. The platform also includes options for users to request a review of their cases if they were previously closed by the Crown Prosecution Service or local police, particularly under the Victims’ Right to Review (VRR) or the Child Sexual Abuse Review Panel (CSARP).

This initiative is part of Operation Beaconport, which was established in November 2025 following Baroness Casey’s audit of group-based child sexual abuse and exploitation. The operation is currently reviewing hundreds of cases where no further action was taken between January 1, 2010, and March 31, 2025. Victims wishing to submit information about previously closed cases involving group-based offending will have their requests reviewed by specially trained officers from the operation.

The launch of IAmReady.org aims to empower survivors by providing them with the necessary tools and support to navigate their experiences and seek justice. For those affected, this resource may represent a significant step towards healing and accountability.

Anyone submitting information about a case has the option to receive updates regarding their request. Chief Constable Becky Riggs, NPCC Lead for Child Protection and Abuse Investigation, said: “Victims and survivors deserve access to clear information, compassionate support and the opportunity to make informed decisions about what feels right for them. “For many victims and survivors, questions can remain long after an investigation has been closed. Finding information or understanding where to turn next can feel overwhelming. “IAmReady has been developed to help people access information and support whenever they feel ready to do so. Most importantly, it gives victims and survivors greater choice and control, allowing them to decide how and when they engage. “Both IAmReady and Operation Beaconport have been developed with victims and survivors at their heart. “Victims and survivors have played an important role in the development of the website, helping to ensure it reflects the needs and priorities of the people it is designed to support. This reflects our commitment to treating every victim and survivor with dignity, compassion and respect.” To find out more about Operation Beaconport, review options and support available, visit IAmReady herehttps://iamready.org.uk/ SUPPORT THE ROCHDALE TIMES: FOLLOW US ON FACEBOOK Got a story? articles.title: Rochdale-London Train Service Proposal Rejected by Regulator
articles.excerpt: The Office of Rail and Road has rejected plans for a direct train service between Rochdale and London Euston, disappointing local MP Paul Waugh and rail operator Lumo.
articles.content_html:
The Office of Rail and Road (ORR) has rejected a proposal for a new train service between Rochdale and London Euston, which aimed to provide four daily return services. The decision has been met with disappointment from Rochdale's MP Paul Waugh and the rail operator Lumo, who had hoped to launch the service by 2028.

The ORR stated that the additional services could increase the risk of delays spreading across the network, ultimately worsening reliability for all passengers. In a statement, Paul Waugh expressed his deep disappointment, highlighting the significance of the service for residents in Rochdale and the surrounding borough. He remains committed to improving transport connections with both Manchester and London.

Waugh noted that there are still reasons for optimism regarding future rail developments. He mentioned the Bee Network, which is set to enhance local rail services across Greater Manchester starting in 2028, and the government's ongoing efforts with Northern Powerhouse Rail, which aims to improve capacity on the West Coast Main Line.

The ORR also rejected similar applications from Wrexham, Shropshire & Midlands Railway Company for Wrexham-London services and Avanti West Coast for additional Blackpool-Euston services. A spokesperson for Lumo indicated that they are considering their next steps following the ORR's decision.

evidence_sources.captured_text: ‘Disappointment’ following Rochdale-London train idea rejected | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch ‘Disappointment’ following Rochdale-London train idea rejected George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 10, 2026 | 8:42 AM Print Land around Rochdale Station The decision to axe the idea for trains between Rochdale and London Euston is ‘disappointing’, says the town’s MP and rail operator. The idea to have four daily return services between Rochdale and London was rejected by the Office of Rail and Road (ORR). The reason given was that the additional services could ‘increase the risk of delays spreading and making reliability of the network worse for all passengers’. Low-cost rail operator Lumo had hoped to start services by 2028, with the plans receiving the backing of Rochdale MP Paul Waugh. Both shared their disappointment following the announcement. Paul Waugh, Rochdale’s MP, said: “I am deeply disappointed that the ORR has rejected the proposal for a direct Rochdale to London service. I know how much this would have meant to people in Rochdale and the wider borough, and I remain committed to improving our connections with both Manchester and London. “There are reasons to be hopeful about the future. The Bee Network is bringing greater integration of local rail services across Greater Manchester from 2028 onwards, while the government is progressing Northern Powerhouse Rail and has set out its long-term intention to develop a new rail connection between Birmingham and Manchester to increase capacity on the West Coast Main Line. “These are important investments in our rail network, and I will continue to make the case for Rochdale to benefit from better and more reliable transport links, including to London.” The ORR explained that gaps in the current timetable provide important space for trains to recover when disruption occurs, minimising delays to passengers. The government body concluded that adding more services into these windows would reduce that resilience and increase risk of disruption. The ORR also rejected the application of Wrexham, Shropshire & Midlands Railway Company (WSMR) for four return Wrexham-London Euston services and Avanti West Coast’s application for additional Blackpool-Euston services. A spokesperson for FirstGroup, who run the Lumo operation, said: “We are disappointed that the ORR has declined our revised application for new Lumo services between London and Rochdale, and we are considering our next steps. “Following the initial decision, we amended our plans in line with feedback and believe the revised proposal demonstrated strong economic benefits for passengers and communities. “It would have delivered the benefits of competition, including greater choice, lower fares and new opportunities for growth across Manchester and the north west. “Open access services have an important role to play in improving connectivity, attracting more people to rail and supporting economic development, all at no cost to the public purse. “We remain convinced that this route offered a compelling case for investment and long-term benefits for communities, businesses and the wider regional economy.” ORR has approved access for Avanti’s weekday 19:29 Chester to Euston service to carry passengers until December 2030. This train already runs as a fully crewed empty service so does not add another train to the route, but will benefit passengers, says the ORR. Stephanie Tobyn, ORR’s director of strategy, policy and reform, said: “New services, destinations and greater choice can bring real benefits for passengers and communities. But the West Coast Main Line is already under significant pressure, with performance reflecting limited resilience on a heavily used part of the rail network. “Our detailed analysis has shown that adding more trains to the current timetable would reduce the ability to recover when disruption occurs, increasing the risk of delays spreading and making reliability of the network worse for all passengers.” Add Roch Valley Radio as a preferred source on Google News to see more of our local reporting Add as a preferred source on Google Do you have a story for us? articles.title: Rochdale's Music Heritage Celebrated in New Album 'Kenion Street'
articles.excerpt: The album 'Kenion Street', believed to be the first commercial release by a UK council, showcases local talent and pays tribute to the town's rich musical history.
articles.content_html:
An album titled 'Kenion Street', believed to be the first commercial release by a UK council, has gained significant attention, reaching millions of listeners on national radio and streaming platforms. Launched as part of Rochdale's year as Greater Manchester Town of Culture, the album features local artists performing reimagined versions of classic tracks recorded at the town's iconic studios.

From 1977 to 2001, Rochdale was home to Suite Sixteen and Cargo Studios, located on Kenion Street, where renowned artists such as OMD, The Stone Roses, Happy Mondays, Joy Division, and Inspiral Carpets recorded some of their most memorable work. The album includes 11 tracks, featuring PoolEra's rendition of OMD's 'Electricity', Medley's version of New Order's 'Dreams Never End', and Jennifer Read's interpretation of The Fall's 'Totally Wired'.

All tracks were recorded and produced at Voltalab Sound Studios, situated in the original Cargo/Suite Sixteen building, by studio founder Jamie Alsop. The album has received positive reviews and was featured on Radio 6 Music, where Middleton band K-Estate's cover of Gang of Four's 'Damaged Goods' was highlighted as Track of the Day. Other tracks have been played across various stations, including XS Manchester and Mersey Radio, reaching a combined audience of over 3.5 million.

The release of 'Kenion Street' not only showcases local talent but also serves as a reminder of Rochdale's significant contribution to the music industry. The album's success may inspire further initiatives to celebrate and promote the town's rich musical heritage.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Album is still banging the drum for town’s music heritage - Rochdale Times Skip to content LATEST NEWS Album is still banging the drum for town’s music heritage An album which is believed to be the first commercial release by a UK council has reached millions of listeners on national radio and streaming platforms. Kenion Street has enjoyed glowing reviews after being launched as part of Rochdale’s year as Greater Manchester Town of Culture. It features local acts performing their version of a classic track originally recorded at iconic studios in the town. From 1977 to 2001, Rochdale was home to both Suite Sixteen and Cargo Studios in Kenion Street, where trailblazing artists including OMD, The Stone Roses, Happy Mondays, Joy Division, Inspiral Carpets, Autechre, A Certain Ratio, The Fall and many others recorded some of their most memorable work. The 11 tracks on Kenion Street included PoolEra’s version of Electricity by OMD, Dreams Never End by New Order re-imagined by Medley, and Jennifer Read’s dramatic version of Totally Wired, by The Fall. Micah Stalgic and choir Local Vocals performing Atmosphere by Joy Division, that features on the album All the new tracks were recorded and produced at Voltalab Sound Studios, based in the original Cargo/Suite Sixteen building in Kenion Street, by studio founder Jamie Alsop. Radio 6 Music also featured the album, playing Middleton band’s K-Estate’s version of Gang of Four’s Damaged Goods. It was also made Track of the Day on Radio X with other tracks played across XS Manchester, Mersey Radio, Phoenix FM and many more, with a combined audience of over 3.5 million. One of the album’s singles by Desyfer and Emma Konnanov — a cover of the Happy Mondays anthem Twenty Four Hour Party People — reached 62 in the official UK singles chart and 58 in the official UK singles download chart. Vinyl copies of the album were distributed to record shops nationwide with listening parties held at Rough Trade stores in London, Liverpool, Bristol and Nottingham. READ MORE: Council urged to call time on rules which stop former pubs reopening The album achieved national media coverage with positive reviews from the likes of Louder Than War, The List and many more. Two bands who featured on the album, Metro and K-Estate, were awarded slots on the main stage at this summer’s Rochdale Feel Good Festival, supporting acts including Gabrielle, Ash and Starsailor. Cllr Sue Smith, cabinet member for culture and co-operation at Rochdale Council, said: “Everyone involved should be so proud of creating this lasting record of an important part of our borough’s story. “Thanks to the album, new audiences have discovered the town’s musical past as well as heard some of our talented acts of today. “Music is so important to Rochdale, not just as a part of its history with Gracie Fields in the 1930s and then in the seventies and early eighties but in more recent decades too with the likes of The Courteeners and Lisa Stansfield. PoolEra perform Electricity by OMD, another classic track originally recorded in Rochdale “In the town where these world-famous artists recorded iconic tracks, it’s great to see how ground-breaking music continues to thrive.” Karen Boardman, music development manager at Rochdale Development Agency, added: “I’m incredibly proud of this record which we believe is the UK’s first commercially released album by a council, celebrating a town’s musical history, whilst championing its new talent. It’s been a privilege to work alongside our partners and all the artists to bring the album to life and I’m very excited for the next phase of this project, there’s lots more to come.” The story continued this summer, with synth-pop icons Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark (OMD) returning to where it began when they performed a sold-out show in front of over 5,000 fans at Rochdale Town Hall Square in August, alongside post-punk legends Peter Hook & The Light, and Manchester’s post-punk/funk band – A Certain Ratio. You can listen to the album ‘Kenion Street’ on streaming platforms or pick up a vinyl copy at Rocks Off in Drake Street in Rochdale and other good record stores. Rochdale Music Stories is a collaboration between Voltalab Sound Studios, Stockport Music Story and Rochdale Development Agency, funded by Arts Council England, Rochdale Borough Council and Rochdale Development Agency. articles.title: Bev Craig and Rochdale: will Greater Manchester's new mayor deliver beyond the city centre?
articles.excerpt: A detailed examination of Mayor Bev Craig's council voting record, Rochdale's deprivation and earnings, affordable housing and transport pledges, and the financial risks behind Greater Manchester's investment plans.
articles.content_html:
Bev Craig's election as Mayor of Greater Manchester leaves Rochdale with a familiar question: will economic growth across the city-region translate into better-paid jobs, more affordable housing and better transport in the boroughs outside Manchester city centre?

Craig, the former leader of Manchester City Council, succeeded Andy Burnham after the mayoral election on 30 July 2026. The official result gave her 309,525 first- and second-preference votes, on a Greater Manchester turnout of 25.14%. Turnout in Rochdale was 22.95%, and she received 15,927 first-preference votes in the borough.

Her pledges on housing, public transport, high streets and industrial regeneration speak directly to several of Rochdale's needs. But the financial distinction between projects approved, investment proposed and outcomes delivered is essential.

ROCHDALE'S DEEPER ECONOMIC PROBLEMS

ONS figures reported through Nomis put Rochdale's employment rate for people aged 16–64 at 67.1% in the year to March 2026, against 75.5% across Great Britain. Estimated unemployment was 7.2%, compared with 4.5% nationally, although the ONS warns that survey-based local unemployment estimates have small-sample limitations.

In 2025, around 33.5% of working-age residents held a qualification at RQF Level 4 or above, compared with 48.6% nationally. The median weekly earnings of full-time employees resident in Rochdale were £689.50, against £766.60 in Great Britain.

According to the Government's 2025 English Indices of Deprivation, Rochdale's employment deprivation measure was 20.3%, among the highest of England's local authorities. A neighbourhood identified as Rochdale 010C has repeatedly appeared among the country's 100 most deprived neighbourhoods.

These figures expose the limitations of equating economic development with prosperity for existing residents. A growing regional economy does not automatically lift household earnings if local people cannot reach the jobs, lack relevant qualifications or cannot afford the homes built nearby.

A MAYOR WITHOUT A PARLIAMENTARY VOTING RECORD

Craig has never served as a Member of Parliament. Burnham was previously the MP for Leigh and a Cabinet minister. Tony Lloyd, the interim Greater Manchester mayor before Burnham, was also an MP.

Craig entered Manchester City Council in 2011 and became its leader in December 2021. Her record must therefore be examined through council and combined-authority decisions, rather than voting divisions or questions in the House of Commons. Attributing parliamentary votes to her would be incorrect.

This distinction is not unusual among English regional mayors. West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker, North East Mayor Kim McGuinness and South Yorkshire Mayor Oliver Coppard had not served as MPs before taking office. The question is what experience of budgets, national negotiations and local delivery each officeholder brings, not whether a Commons career is a qualification for office.

WHAT HER COUNCIL DECISIONS SHOW

While Craig led Manchester City Council, the authority approved a 2026/27 revenue budget exceeding £1 billion and a 4.99% council tax increase, incorporating a 2% adult social care element. The council said this supported existing services, investment in communities, housing and public provision.

At the Greater Manchester Combined Authority meeting on 13 February 2026, the authority endorsed a Band D mayoral general precept of £153.95: £92.20 relating to fire and rescue and £61.75 to other mayoral functions. The decision followed a named unanimous vote. Compared with the previous year, the Band D precept rose £25.

These decisions were collective, and the latter was a proposal originally brought by Burnham, not a unilateral Craig tax policy. Nevertheless, the record is relevant when evaluating promises to reduce household costs and decisions about how services are paid for.

Craig was also a portfolio lead on the Greater Manchester Good Growth Fund and integrated investment pipeline approved in November 2025. The authority reported initial potential investment capacity in excess of £1 billion and approved borrowing of up to £150 million against future retained business rates.

The phrase '£1 billion investment' should not be mistaken for £1 billion in unencumbered grants. Parts of the programme involve repayable finance, borrowing or contributions from other institutions. How much is ultimately invested, and where, is more meaningful than the initial headline figure.

AFFORDABLE HOUSING: WHAT DOES THE PROMISE MEAN FOR ROCHDALE?

Craig has pledged 50,000 council, social and genuinely affordable homes across Greater Manchester by 2039, including 10,000 homes delivered, under construction or in the pipeline by May 2028.

The three categories in that near-term target are not equivalent. A completed home can be occupied. A home under construction may still face delivery risks. A home in the pipeline may lack full financing or planning approval.

Over roughly 13 years, 50,000 homes implies an average of nearly 3,850 annually across the region, although actual delivery is unlikely to be evenly spread. The programme relies on public and private land, delivery partners and capital funding that will vary from scheme to scheme.

Rochdale needs published borough-specific targets, a social-rent breakdown, site-by-site funding and delivery dates. 'Affordable' as a statutory housing designation is not always affordable for a household on below-average wages.

TRANSPORT: AN AREA WHERE THE MAYOR HAS DIRECT SPENDING CHOICES

Burnham's transport legacy includes the Bee Network and bringing local buses under public control. Craig has committed to extending free Bee Network bus travel to young people aged 11–16, building on the existing scheme for those aged 16–18.

Transport for Greater Manchester estimates that nearly 200,000 young people could benefit, saving families up to about £500 per eligible child a year. The proposed start date is January 2027, but detailed eligibility and the formal decision process have yet to be completed. The combined authority's forward plan lists a relevant decision for November 2026.

There is a financial trade-off: cheaper travel can widen access to education and employment, while recurring concessions can create continuing expenditure or foregone fare income. An annual programme budget, estimates of extra journeys and bus capacity would make the policy's cost clearer.

Meanwhile, Rochdale, Heywood and Middleton have longstanding demands for stronger rail and tram links. Early development funding for the Oldham–Rochdale–Heywood–Bury tram-train concept should not be confused with an approved construction budget.

In a September 2026 parliamentary answer to Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell, the Department for Transport confirmed that Greater Manchester is due £2.5 billion in Transport for City Regions funding between 2027/28 and 2031/32, and that scheme prioritisation rests with the mayor. That does not mean all of the money is free for the tram proposal: other regional transport commitments compete for the same settlement.

MIDDLETON AND ATOM VALLEY

Middleton is a practical test of whether investment can extend beyond Manchester's commercial centre.

On 25 September 2026, the GMCA approved the proposed designation of a Middleton mayoral development area, subject to the borough council's consent. Rochdale Council Cabinet endorsed the plans on 29 September. The proposed Middleton Co-operative Mayoral Development Corporation is intended to coordinate land, investment and regeneration.

A development corporation can help assemble and develop sites, but the designation alone creates neither jobs nor homes. Residents will need to know the initial public expenditure, which businesses are being attracted and whether vacant premises are being brought into productive use.

Atom Valley and plans for a Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre offer the possibility of advanced manufacturing employment in Rochdale. Earlier GMCA proposals included an indicative allocation of up to £15 million for the centre. Indicative funding, however, is not evidence that the whole scheme has been built or that local recruitment benefits have been achieved.

Craig's proposed £20 million Good Growth High Streets Fund raises a similar question. Although a simple division across Greater Manchester's ten boroughs would imply £2 million each, that is not the fund's published allocation mechanism. The official forward plan schedules the launch decision for 13 November 2026. Its distribution and final conditions remain important.

IS THE ECONOMIC PROGRAMME FINANCIALLY FEASIBLE?

Three kinds of promise require different financial tests: ongoing services, one-off capital construction and investment meant to generate repayments or returns.

Transport concessions may need continuing annual support. Housing and infrastructure require capital, planning approvals, land and delivery partners. Investment financed by borrowing must produce enough income or wider economic benefit to justify financing costs and risk.

The Good Growth Fund's capacity incorporates future retained business-rates income and borrowing, so its published performance should be judged against debt-service costs, reserves, expected returns and delays. Lower-than-expected project returns could restrict later investment capacity.

There is an economic case for public intervention where contaminated land, weak connectivity or low private returns prevent development. Equally, a funding announcement does not remove the possibility of construction inflation, overruns or weak returns.

None of these observations establishes that Craig's programme is either fully financed or unaffordable. An authoritative judgement requires programme-level budgets that separate committed grants from lending, approved borrowing from available cash, and announced schemes from projects ready to proceed.

HOW OTHER REGIONS ARE APPROACHING THE SAME QUESTIONS

The West Midlands, with a broadly comparable metropolitan scale, has pursued a mix of housing, regeneration and transport investment under Richard Parker. Its announced Futures Fund draws on several funding and investment partners rather than operating simply as a direct grant pot.

In Liverpool City Region, Steve Rotheram has pursued bus franchising and integrated transport, while South Yorkshire's Oliver Coppard has combined transport reform with access to skills and work. Their regions differ in population, devolved powers, infrastructure and financial structure, making simplistic headline spending comparisons unreliable.

For Greater Manchester, much of the institutional machinery was developed under Burnham: bus franchising, devolved transport decisions, investment coordination and city-region policy-making. Craig inherits that machinery rather than beginning from scratch.

WHAT THE BOROUGH SHOULD BE ABLE TO MEASURE

Rochdale residents should be able to see investment figures broken down by borough and funding type; affordable homes completed and their rents; local recruitment and wages on public-backed schemes; transport projects with approved construction budgets; and the proportion of high-street funding that actually reaches each community.

The same applies to Atom Valley and Middleton. How many genuinely new posts are created? How many go to Rochdale residents? How much public borrowing is involved? Which sites have actually begun construction?

Craig has made commitments that address recognisable challenges in Rochdale. Some draw on programmes already in progress; others remain targets or proposals requiring further approval. The economically meaningful comparison with Burnham and mayors elsewhere will be based on achieved outcomes and published finances, not the number of projects announced.

For Rochdale, the fundamental test is whether city-region investment reaches households facing lower wages, weaker employment prospects and inadequate transport connections — and whether the financial costs of delivering it remain transparent.

articles.title: Overnight Road Closures Planned at Sudden Junction, Rochdale from October 12 to 15
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council will implement overnight road closures around Sudden Junction from October 12 to 15 for resurfacing work, affecting traffic routes and diversions.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced that overnight road closures will take place around Sudden Junction from Monday, October 12, to Thursday, October 15. The closures are necessary for resurfacing work, which will include refreshing road markings and renewing traffic signs.

The affected roads will be closed nightly between 8pm and 5am. Manchester Road in Castleton will be closed northbound between Onslow Street and Bolton Road, impacting traffic heading towards Rochdale town centre. Additionally, Silk Street will operate as one-way towards Tesco, preventing drivers from travelling from Tesco towards Manchester Road. Traffic on Bolton Road will also be restricted from turning right onto Manchester Road towards Castleton.

In a statement, the council confirmed that fully signed diversion routes will be in place to guide motorists during the closures. The resurfacing work aims to improve road safety and traffic flow in the area, which has seen increased usage in recent months.

Motorists are advised to plan their journeys accordingly and allow extra time for travel during the closure period. The council will continue to provide updates as the work progresses.

articles.title: Ofsted Releases Inspection Reports for Greenbank Primary and Meadows Schools in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Ofsted has published new inspection reports for Greenbank Primary School and Meadows School, both located in Rochdale, detailing their findings and ratings.
articles.content_html:
Ofsted has published new inspection reports for Greenbank Primary School and Meadows School, both located in Rochdale, on 9 October 2026. The reports outline the findings from the inspections and any ratings awarded to the schools.

Greenbank Primary School's report indicates the school's performance and areas for improvement, although specific ratings were not detailed in the summary. The inspection process typically occurs every four years unless there are concerns that necessitate an earlier review. Parents and guardians can access the latest data for Greenbank Primary through the Ofsted website and are encouraged to participate in the Ofsted Parent View Survey to share their experiences.

Similarly, Meadows School's report provides insights into its operational standards and educational quality. Ofsted inspects non-association independent schools every three years, with additional inspections conducted when commissioned by the Secretary of State for Education. The report aims to inform parents about the school's performance and help them make informed decisions regarding their children's education.

Both schools are encouraged to use the feedback from these inspections to enhance their educational offerings. Parents interested in the reports can find them on the Ofsted website, where they can also subscribe for alerts regarding future inspections. For any inquiries, parents are advised to contact the schools directly.

articles.title: Mayor Faisal Rana visits Rochdale Sixth Form College to see student support and results
articles.excerpt: Mayor Faisal Rana and the Mayoress visited Rochdale Sixth Form College, highlighting its student support, pastoral provision and recent academic achievements.
articles.content_html: Mayor Faisal Rana and the Mayoress have visited Rochdale Sixth Form College, meeting Principal Karl Smith and touring the college to see its facilities and student support. The visit included the Achievement Centre, which provides additional support for students who may be falling behind or need extra help with their studies. The Mayor and Mayoress also visited the student café and highlighted the college's focus on pastoral support, attendance and punctuality. ### College results and progression Rochdale Sixth Form College says its students achieved strong results in 2026. The college's website describes it as one of the country's strongest sixth form colleges for student progress, while its latest results announcement reported exceptional A-level and BTEC outcomes. The college also says around 80% of its students progress to higher education and that it has retained an Outstanding Ofsted judgement. The college's website currently highlights students progressing to Oxford and Cambridge, including former Oulder Hill student Joseph, who achieved three A*s and an A* in his EPQ before progressing to Cambridge, and former Hollingworth student Summer, who achieved four A*s and an A* in her EPQ before progressing to Oxford. Faisal Rana said the visit was particularly meaningful because four of his children had attended the college and achieved what he described as exceptional results. He said the visit offered a different perspective on the college, beyond that of a parent. He also praised the college's emphasis on supporting students, raising aspirations and creating opportunities for young people in the borough. Principal Karl Smith hosted the visit. Source: Faisal Rana, Mayor of Rochdale; Rochdale Sixth Form College. articles.title: RBH football team takes part in Housing Association Charity Cup 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing colleagues took part in the Housing Association Charity Cup 2026 after weeks of training, with the team already looking ahead to next year's tournament.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Boroughwide Housing's football team joined eight other housing providers for the Housing Association Charity Cup 2026 at Goals Manchester.

The tournament followed weeks of preparation from RBH colleagues, who gave up their own time to train every Wednesday at the Soccer Factory in Castleton.

While Team RBH did not bring home the trophy, the organisation said the tournament was a successful opportunity for colleagues to come together and enjoy some friendly competition.

Salix Homes won the 2026 cup, while RBH congratulated everyone who took part and represented the organisation.

### Looking ahead to next year

RBH thanked Chris Hudspith, its Multi Trade Co-ordinator, for arranging the training sessions and encouraging colleagues to get involved.

Hudspith said the football programme had been a positive experience and an opportunity to meet people from other teams and departments while taking part in a shared interest.

Martin Platt, an IT Trainer, said the team came away from the tournament feeling that some close games could have gone differently, adding that they hoped to return next year and win the trophy.

RBH also said it is hoping to have a women's team competing in next year's tournament.

articles.title: Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit highlights opportunities for local businesses
articles.excerpt: Businesses and organisations gathered at the Crown Oil Arena for the Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit, with discussions focused on accessing contracts, bidding and local economic growth.
articles.content_html:
Businesses and organisations from across the borough have come together for the Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit, with discussions focused on how local firms can access procurement opportunities and grow their businesses.

The event was organised by the Rochdale Development Agency and held at the newly refurbished Crown Oil Arena, home of Rochdale AFC.

The summit brought together organisations involved in procurement, regeneration and business support, including STAR Procurement, Match My Project, Hopwood Hall College, Willmott Dixon and the Rochdale Development Agency.

Discussions focused on how businesses can get onto the procurement ladder, understand the bidding process and position themselves to compete for contracts and opportunities with larger organisations.

Mayor Faisal Rana, who attended the event, said greater collaboration between local businesses and organisations delivering investment across the borough was important to ensuring local firms can benefit from upcoming opportunities.

He highlighted figures from the Rochdale Development Agency's latest independent economic impact assessment, which it says found that its work had created, supported or safeguarded 765 jobs and supported 699 businesses. The assessment also reported £14.30 in local economic value for every £1 invested.

The mayor also pointed to major investment programmes including Atom Valley, the Rochdale Rail Corridor, town centre regeneration, housing and skills investment as areas where businesses could potentially benefit from future procurement and supply-chain opportunities.

The summit comes as public-sector and regeneration projects continue to create demand for contractors, suppliers and other local businesses across a range of sectors.

The Rochdale Development Agency and organisations involved in procurement are encouraging businesses to understand the opportunities available and build their capacity to bid for work.

The event also underlined the potential economic impact of keeping a greater share of investment within the local economy, through jobs, business growth and local supply chains.

The Rochdale AFC Community Trust was also associated with the event.

articles.title: Roadworks Scheduled on Well i' th' Lane in Rochdale from 24 October 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has announced roadworks on Well i' th' Lane starting 24 October 2026, with alternative routes provided for motorists.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced that roadworks will commence on Well i' th' Lane from 12 midnight on Saturday, 24 October 2026, continuing until 11.59pm on Sunday, 1 November 2026. During this period, part of the road will be temporarily closed to facilitate the necessary works.

Motorists travelling southbound will be diverted via Queen Victoria Street, Oldham Road, and Queensway. The council advises drivers to plan their journeys accordingly to avoid delays during the roadworks.

In addition to Well i' th' Lane, several other roads in the Rochdale area will also undergo maintenance. Notably, Willbutts Lane and Rooley Street will see roadworks starting on 12 October 2026, with closures expected to last for a maximum of 21 days. Willbutts Lane will be closed at the junction with Edenfield Road, extending 14 metres westward, while Rooley Street will be closed at the same junction, extending 10 metres eastward.

Egerton Street in Heywood will also be closed from 12 midnight on Tuesday, 20 October 2026, until 11.59pm on Sunday, 1 November 2026, with the closure beginning at the junction with Hind Hill Street and extending 165 metres westward. Residents and commuters are encouraged to check the Rochdale Borough Council's website for further details, including maps of the affected areas and updates on the roadworks.

articles.title: Man arrested on suspicion of murder after man found deceased on Curzon Road
articles.excerpt: Greater Manchester Police has arrested a man on suspicion of murder after a man was found deceased at an address on Curzon Road, Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of murder following the death of a man at an address on Curzon Road, Rochdale.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said officers received a report of a concern for the welfare of a man at an address on Curzon Road at around 7.55pm on Wednesday 7 October 2026.

Emergency services attended and the man was sadly confirmed deceased at the scene.

A man in his 40s has been arrested on suspicion of murder and remains in police custody for questioning.

GMP said an investigation is underway to establish the circumstances surrounding the death and that detectives are exploring all lines of enquiry.

The man's next of kin have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.

Detective Superintendent Richard Hunt said: “Firstly, our thoughts remain with the family of the man who sadly died, and we have officers assigned to support them through this difficult time.

“An investigation is underway and officers are working at pace to establish the circumstances which led to this man’s death.

“We currently have a man in custody for questioning and ask the public to refrain from speculating at this time. This is a live investigation, and we are currently exploring all avenues of enquiry and keeping an open mind.”

No finding of guilt should be inferred from an arrest or allegation. The arrested man remains under investigation and is presumed innocent unless and until convicted.

Source: Greater Manchester Police.

articles.title: Remembrance and reflection walks offer bereaved service families a place to connect at Denehurst Park
articles.excerpt: Get Together After Serving CIC invites families, partners and loved ones to a gentle weekly remembrance walk at Denehurst Park in Rochdale, with no pressure to talk about loss.
articles.content_html:
A weekly remembrance walk in Rochdale is offering families and loved ones of fallen service personnel a chance to find companionship, fresh air and a little space to reflect.

Organised by Get Together After Serving CIC (G.A.S-CIC), the Remembrance & Reflection Walk takes place every Wednesday at Denehurst Park. Participants are invited to meet outside Denehurst Café at 12.30pm before setting off together.

The gentle walk is expected to last between 30 minutes and an hour, depending on the weather. Dogs are very welcome, although there is no need to bring one to take part.

At the heart of the initiative is the understanding that grief does not always need words. Those attending can share memories of someone they have lost, chat about everyday life, walk quietly or simply enjoy being in the company of people who understand.

The event poster captures that sentiment: “Sometimes you don’t need a meeting or a support group. Sometimes you just need to get outside, walk, talk and spend some time with people who understand.”

After the walk, the group plans to return to Denehurst Café for a warm drink, a slice of cake and more time together for anyone who wishes to stay.

The invitation is aimed at families and loved ones remembering fallen heroes, with partners and friends also welcome. There is no expectation to discuss personal experiences or bereavement, and those who would prefer a quiet walk will be just as welcome as those looking for conversation.

The weekly gathering brings remembrance into the everyday: not only formal ceremonies or anniversaries, but a simple opportunity to come together, one Wednesday at a time.

Walk details: Every Wednesday at 12.30pm. Meeting point: outside Denehurst Café, Denehurst Park, Rochdale. The walk lasts 30 minutes to one hour, weather permitting. Dogs are welcome, but are not required. Participants can return to the café afterwards for optional refreshments and company.

articles.title: Sara Rowbotham: the Rochdale health worker who raised 181 safeguarding alerts
articles.excerpt: Sara Rowbotham repeatedly raised concerns about vulnerable young people while working for Rochdale’s Crisis Intervention Team, later giving evidence to Parliament about the response to child sexual exploitation in the town.
articles.content_html:
Sara Rowbotham became one of the most recognisable figures associated with the response to child sexual exploitation in Rochdale after repeatedly raising concerns about vulnerable young people while working for the town’s NHS Crisis Intervention Team.

Rowbotham worked as the Crisis Intervention Team Co-ordinator and Sexual Health Improvement Specialist. The team was established in 2004 and supported thousands of young people, including those who disclosed concerns about sexual abuse and exploitation.

In evidence to the House of Commons Home Affairs Committee in November 2012, Rowbotham told MPs that, over a period covering the years from 2005 to 2011, her team had identified referrals involving 103 young people.

She also told the committee that she had made 181 alerts to Children’s Social Care about concerns involving young people.

Asked whether she believed police and social services had worked together effectively, Rowbotham said this had happened “very rarely” in the early period and that she had subsequently begun making the Safeguarding Children Unit aware of the referrals so that strategy meetings could be convened.

The committee also heard evidence from other senior officials about the handling of the information. The subsequent Home Affairs Committee report described missed opportunities and examined the response of children's social care and police to child sexual exploitation in Rochdale.

Rowbotham told MPs that she had repeatedly tried to make protective services aware of the vulnerability of young people and that she believed agencies had failed to provide a sufficiently comprehensive and coordinated response.

The evidence came after the prosecution of nine men in Rochdale in 2012 for serious sexual offences against girls. The case prompted wider scrutiny of how authorities had responded to reports of child sexual exploitation.

Rowbotham continued to speak publicly about the response. In 2014, she was made redundant from her role. Contemporary reporting by ITV News and The Guardian documented her concerns about the handling of the case and the impact of losing her position.

Her story later reached a much wider audience when the BBC drama Three Girls was broadcast in May 2017, with Maxine Peake portraying Rowbotham.

A petition calling for Rowbotham to be formally recognised attracted more than 100,000 signatures within days of the programme airing and ultimately exceeded 275,000 signatures, according to contemporary reports.

Rowbotham subsequently entered local politics. She was elected as a councillor for North Middleton in 2015 and went on to serve as Deputy Leader of Rochdale Borough Council and as a cabinet member.

Her public recognition also continued. She received a Special Recognition Award at the NHS Heroes Awards in 2018 and was made an honorary member of the NSPCC Council that year. In 2021, she was appointed MBE for services to young people.

Rowbotham’s evidence to Parliament remains part of the official record of the scrutiny that followed the Rochdale child sexual exploitation cases. Her account of the 181 alerts, and questions about how information held by frontline services was acted upon, formed part of the wider examination of safeguarding failures in the town.

Source: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee evidence and report; contemporary reporting by ITV News and The Guardian; Rochdale Borough Council records.
